strategy.headline: Sell New Orleans first and the Pelicans second: paid, hand-made craft on the city's own clock.
strategy.thesis: New Orleans fans wear the city before the team: Dirty Coast and Fleurty Girl phrase tees, ward numbers and school colors beat a Pelicans logo that only dates to 2013. This is a town that watched the Jazz leave and the Hornets spend two Katrina seasons in Oklahoma City. The city keeps its own clock, and it matches the NBA season almost exactly. Second lines run Sundays from Labor Day to June, king cake from Jan 6 to Mardi Gras on Feb 9, 2027, and crawfish from Lent through Jazz Fest. After a 26-56 season, with first-year coach Jamahl Mosley and no 2026 first-round pick, the standings won't sell product, but craft and calendar will. Make roughly two-thirds of units city-first with a secondary Pelicans mark, and one-third player and team product. Commission the city's hands (sign painters, brass bands, bounce artists, school programs) on their terms, and drop on New Orleans dates, not league dates.

archetype.name: The Second Line
archetype.description: They dance behind the city's main line of Saints, LSU and Carnival. They stayed loyal through two lost franchises and get loud when the music is right. They buy city pride first and team gear second, and they punish anything that reads tourist.

pulse.teamMoment: New coach Jamahl Mosley inherits a 26-56 team after a quiet offseason under Joe Dumars. He gets Zion Williamson, breakout scorer Trey Murphy III (21.5 ppg, kept through June trade rumors) and second-years Derik Queen and Jeremiah Fears. The Pelicans aren't on the opening-night or Christmas slates. Their early-season stage is NBA Cup West Group B (OKC, MIN, LAC, MEM), which opens Oct 30 at the Clippers.
pulse.sentiment: Weary, not angry. Fans are protective of Murphy, hopeful on Queen and Fears, and cautious about building anything on Zion's availability. The "NOLA Nights" Skelican City Edition excites them more than the roster does. It came back in 2025-26, though the 2026-27 design is unverified.

topInsights.title: City mark first, team mark second
topInsights.insight: Locals wear local phrase tees over team gear, and the Pelicans fight Saints black-and-gold and LSU purple-and-gold for the same shirt drawer. The 2023-24 "NOLA Nights" City Edition (purple, neon green and the skeletal Skelican) came back in 2025-26. It showed that a New Orleans-after-dark story beats the standard marks.
topInsights.implication: Make every hero piece pass as New Orleans pride on the street. Put the Pelicans mark on a secondary lockup, jock tag or sleeve hit. Keep a lean one-third of units team- and player-led.

topInsights.title: The NBA season is second-line season
topInsights.insight: Social Aid & Pleasure Clubs parade most Sundays from Labor Day into June. They turn out in new color-matched suits and fresh sneakers, the city's living fashion show, and keep their colors secret until parade day. No other NBA market has a weekly street-style ritual on the same calendar as its home schedule.
topInsights.implication: Build tonal, color-matchable sneaker and warm-up sets for the general line. Treat any club collaboration as the club's project: paid, credited, and released only if and when the club wants.

topInsights.title: Carnival color is tourist shorthand, craft isn't
topInsights.insight: Purple, green and gold is on every souvenir in the Quarter, and it blurs into LSU. Even the team's fan-favorite City Edition went with purple and neon green at night instead. What locals haven't seen on a jersey is the hand-made civic city: blue-and-white tile street names, sign painters' dot-bordered lettering, iron lace and brass-band drum heads.
topInsights.implication: Use commissioned craft (tile numerals, hand-lettered alphabets, iron-lace jacquard, brushed-brass hardware) as the design system, and keep Carnival color to small January accents.

topInsights.title: Food is the most precise retail clock
topInsights.insight: Pelicans attention peaks October to December. Then the city's own seasons take over: king cake from Jan 6 to Feb 9, fish fries and crawfish from Ash Wednesday (Feb 10) into May, and sno-balls all summer. The team already has the season's best inside joke, the King Cake Baby.
topInsights.implication: Sequence drops by what's on the table: a king cake knit on Jan 6, a crawfish-red pack from late February, and nectar-cream pink for spring and summer. Never launch a hero drop in the final two weeks before Mardi Gras.

topInsights.title: Identity is ward, school and side of the river
topInsights.insight: New Orleanians place each other by high school ('What school you went to?') and by ward, and bounce records shout out wards by number. The West Bank and New Orleans East rep separately. School programs like St. Aug and Edna Karr, and HBCUs like Xavier, Dillard and Southern, carry more block-level loyalty than a losing pro team.
topInsights.implication: Build modular ward and side-of-the-river product first, drawn by artists from each area. Phase in school and HBCU co-brands through each institution's own licensing office.

topInsights.title: Permanence beats promises
topInsights.insight: Basketball has left New Orleans twice. So in a 26-56 season, fans worry less about wins than about whether the team is rooted here. Murphy is the player they trust, and Zion is the most famous name (and a Jordan Brand athlete). The brown pelican itself came back from near-zero after DDT, a comeback story nobody has put on product.
topInsights.implication: Tell 'still here' stories (pelican in her piety liners, ward and school ties), not contention messaging. Lead player product with whichever young players Nike actually has relationships with.

topInsights.title: The sacred line is the credibility test
topInsights.insight: Black Masking Indian suits, chants and patches are sacred and individually authored. Second-line regalia belongs to its clubs. Bounce was built by queer Black artists such as Katey Red and Sissy Nobby. This city beat the NFL over the 'Who Dat' letters in 2010, and it calls out brands that borrow without paying.
topInsights.implication: Pay up front and credit by name. Never print or trace Indian beadwork. Get consent from each club, band and artist directly, not through a single gatekeeper.

opportunities.title: Twelfth Night Pack
opportunities.summary: The season's biggest city-specific drop, released Jan 6 as king cake season and Carnival begin. Picture a navy ground with a fine sanding-sugar fleck, doubloon jock tags and, if cleared, the King Cake Baby. Skip the beads, masks and block Carnival color.
where: Pelicans Team Store, Smoothie King Center
Fleurty Girl (French Quarter, Lakeside Metairie and Gretna doors)
opportunities.when: Launch Jan 6 and run through Mardi Gras Day (Feb 9, 2027). Restock by mid-January, and start no new hero launch after about Jan 26.
opportunities.how: Ship the pack in a king-cake-style box. Give away paid Dong Phuong king cake slices at a Carnival-season home night instead of bundling cake with retail. Put the baby on a waistband tab only after the Pelicans confirm they own it and it's cleared for apparel. Otherwise, use a plain plastic-baby silhouette drawn fresh.
products: Sanding-sugar knit warm-up (navy ground, small fleck)
opportunities.segment: Diehard locals, families and Carnival visitors
opportunities.kpi: Sell-through of 50% on entry tees and 35% on premium knits by Feb 1, and January Pelicans revenue versus January 2026

opportunities.title: Ward Call, phased
opportunities.summary: A modular identity line: tile-set ward numerals plus West Bank and The East pieces, each drawn by a paid artist from that area. It launches small and widens across the season.
opportunities.when: Phase one lands at the first confirmed home game after Oct 30, with three areas: 7th Ward, West Bank and The East. The full ward set rolls out December to February. School co-brands wait for a 2027-28 phase two.
opportunities.how: Open with a paid, rotating bounce lineup for an arena ward-by-ward call-and-response. Offer it first to pioneers such as Katey Red, Sissy Nobby and DJ Jubilee, and credit the artists on the hangtag and the scoreboard. Add Big Freedia only after her footwear and apparel obligations are cleared.
opportunities.segment: Neighborhood locals, West Bank and East families, and young hoopers
opportunities.kpi: Units by ward code, share sold outside Orleans Parish core doors, and repeat buyers across two or more drops

opportunities.title: Still Here holiday core
opportunities.summary: Capture the year's peak attention, November through December, with accessible city and kids product and a 'still here' piety story. Make player pieces only for names whose apparel status is confirmed.
opportunities.when: Confirmed Friday Cup home nights between Oct 30 and Nov 27, Black Friday, and through Dec 24
opportunities.how: Bundle a kids swingman with a ward tee at a value price. Use one 'Friday night in New Orleans' giveaway graphic that works against any Cup opponent. Add a navy warm-up whose pelican-in-her-piety liner explains the name. Route any Zion piece through Jordan Brand.
opportunities.segment: Families, gift buyers and Gulf South regional fans
opportunities.kpi: Holiday units versus 2025, kids share of jersey sales, and city-first versus player unit mix against the two-thirds plan

opportunities.title: HBCU and school-pride nights
opportunities.summary: Ride the city's two biggest school-pride peaks: Bayou Classic weekend for HBCU fans and the LHSAA basketball playoffs for high school families. The institutions are the licensors and the beneficiaries.
where: Xavier (Gert Town) and Dillard (Gentilly) campus events
opportunities.when: Bayou Classic weekend, Nov 27-28, 2026 (Thanksgiving weekend, pending the Pelicans schedule). Plus a Friday home game during the LHSAA playoffs, February to early March.
opportunities.how: For Classic weekend, build an HBCU-coded capsule licensed through Southern's and Grambling's own programs. Do the same through Xavier and Dillard for a local HBCU night. For high schools, start with one willing program or alumni association and route it through its athletic and licensing office. Make gear or gym funding the headline.
opportunities.segment: HBCU alumni and fans, high school families and Bayou Classic visitors
opportunities.kpi: Attendance and sales on HBCU and school nights, dollars returned to programs, and whether a second school asks in

opportunities.title: Brass series
opportunities.summary: Treat Pelicans Gold as sousaphone brass: foil, hardware and drum-head lettering credited to a named brass band. Pair each drop with instruments for school bands.
where: Maple Leaf Bar and Tipitina's (launch events)
opportunities.when: Launch at a December home game outside Classic weekend, with a second wave after Mardi Gras.
opportunities.how: Lead with Rebirth Brass Band if its members' deals clear. Credit the band on the product, and fund instruments through the Tipitina's Foundation or The Roots of Music. A separate, paid St. Augustine Marching 100 story can headline a home night, credited as a high school program, not an HBCU one.
opportunities.kpi: Sell-through by drop and instruments funded

opportunities.title: Second Line Sunday pilot
opportunities.summary: A first-season pilot with no product. Pay one Social Aid & Pleasure Club and its brass band to bring a second line to a Sunday home game, credited by name. The club decides whether product ever follows.
where: Smoothie King Center, a Sunday home game
opportunities.when: Agree terms in September and October. The arena second line runs on a Sunday home date the club chooses.
opportunities.how: Get the club's written consent directly, and pay the club and band. Route any parade fee support through a culture-bearer intermediary the club picks. If the club later asks for product, make a small, numbered, club-owned run on its timeline, with the swoosh kept off its regalia.
products: Club-owned numbered set only if the club asks
opportunities.segment: Second-line culture and style-led Black New Orleanians
opportunities.kpi: The club's public endorsement and whether another club asks to be next

opportunities.title: Boil Season and Nectar Cream
opportunities.summary: Give the post-Carnival stretch and summer their own palette in heat-ready mesh: boiled-crawfish red, nectar-cream pink and seersucker. Take one event to the city's outdoor courts.
where: Joe W. Brown Memorial Park (New Orleans East) and Behrman Park (Algiers)
opportunities.when: Late February, after Ash Wednesday (Feb 10), through Jazz Fest, then summer. Avoid the March Super Sundays and St. Joseph's Night (Mar 19).
opportunities.how: Launch Boil Season around the team's actual home schedule, and print a Play-In tee only if the team gets there. Then switch to Nectar Cream with a paid sno-ball stand collab. Run a summer court day at Joe W. Brown or Behrman with mesh and sleeveless product. In the Jazz Fest window, drop a poster-style tee from a paid Black New Orleans artist, with no festival marks.
opportunities.segment: Locals in festival season, summer hoopers and spring visitors
opportunities.kpi: March-to-May Pelicans apparel revenue versus 2026 and court-event youth reach

opportunities.title: Claiborne Oaks artist capsule at Essence
opportunities.summary: An artist-owned capsule, offered as an invitation. A Black New Orleans painter renders the live oaks the I-10 overpass removed from Claiborne Avenue, and it launches to the national audience at Essence Festival.
opportunities.when: Essence Festival of Culture, July 4 weekend 2027
opportunities.how: Invite BMike Odums or another Tremé or Seventh Ward artist, with a real option to decline. The artist owns the work, the credit and the choice of Claiborne Corridor beneficiary. Keep it off the uniform and away from Aug 29.
products: Premium hoodie with oak side panels
opportunities.segment: The national Black audience at Essence and culture-led locals
opportunities.kpi: Essence-weekend revenue, out-of-state share of buyers, and dollars returned to the corridor

collection.name: Made by Hand
collection.story: New Orleans marks its identity by hand: tiles at every street corner, sign painters' lettering, sousaphone brass, king cake sugar and the crawfish table. This collection is made with the people who make those things, credited and paid. A Pelicans fan wears the city's own handwriting, not a souvenir.

themes.name: Corner Tile
themes.story: Every New Orleanian knows their corner by its blue-and-white tile street name. This theme sets wards, neighborhoods and numbers in that tile grid for 2026-27 lifestyle product.
themes.graphics: Square-tile block capitals with a tile border for TREMÉ, 7TH WARD, WESTBANK and THE EAST, plus a crescent-and-star water-meter roundel as a quiet secondary mark.
themes.materials: Heavyweight cotton jersey with a glazed-look high-density print, debossed rubber crescent-and-star patches, and Dri-FIT mesh for the shooting shirts.

pieces.detail: One area per tee in tile type, drawn with a paid artist from that ward.
Short-sleeve cobalt mesh with glazed-white tile-grid numbers and a tile-border hem.
A youth cut with the neighborhood name and a hidden pelican tile.
Debossed water-meter roundel on the front, ward number on the side.

themes.name: Brass and Iron
themes.story: Pelicans Gold already reads as a tarnished sousaphone bell. This theme pairs brass-band hardware and drum-head lettering with original iron-lace patterning.
themes.segment: Music-first locals, band culture and premium buyers
themes.graphics: Circular drum-head lockups lettered by a New Orleans sign painter, and an original iron-lace railing drawing with a hidden 'NO' monogram.
themes.materials: Brushed-brass zipper pulls, aglets and snaps, laser-cut iron-lace perforations, tonal jacquard knit, and satin taping.

pieces.detail: Laser-cut lace panels at the yoke with brushed-brass hardware.
A credited brass band's name arched over a circular sign-painted lockup.
Pelicans Gold foil wordmark and a brass drawcord tip.
Tonal lace side panel with the monogram in the scrollwork.
Braid and cross-belt trim co-created with a paid, licensing band program.

themes.name: Twelfth Night
themes.story: King cake sanding sugar as a fine fleck on a navy ground: glitter on dark, not flat Carnival blocks. Doubloons and, if cleared, the King Cake Baby hide inside.
themes.graphics: A sparse sugar-crystal fleck on navy, two-sided doubloon jock tags with a new theme each season, and a small baby or doubloon on the waistband tab.
themes.materials: Navy knit with a metallic-fleck yarn at under 10% coverage, and anodized-aluminum two-sided doubloon tags.

pieces.detail: Navy body with a sparse tri-color crystal fleck and a doubloon pull.
A baby or doubloon on the waistband tab and a doubloon on the leg.
Navy tee with a printed doubloon and the season's theme.
A numbered set of Pelicans doubloons made with a local doubloon maker.

themes.name: Boil Season
themes.story: The stretch run and summer, in the colors of the newspaper-covered crawfish table and the nectar-cream sno-ball. Built for 80°F festival days and outdoor courts.
themes.segment: Festival-season locals, spring visitors and summer hoopers
themes.graphics: A newsprint-grain texture under crawfish red (with no real mastheads), hand-painted sno-ball-stand menu lettering, and navy-and-white seersucker stripes.
themes.materials: Perforated mesh, quick-dry woven, navy-and-white seersucker panels, and packable water-resistant shells.

pieces.detail: Perforated mesh with a newsprint-grain sleeve and navy numerals.
Open-hole mesh in boil red for summer runs at Joe W. Brown and Behrman.
Seersucker side panels on a navy mesh body.
Pink footbed, navy strap and a hand-lettered 'nectar' hit.
Navy shell with a nectar-pink lining that packs into its own pocket.

uniform.narrative: At almost every corner in the city, the street name is set in blue-and-white tile in the sidewalk, and every New Orleanian has stood on theirs. The jersey spells NEW ORLEANS tile by tile in glazed white on a cobalt body and wraps it in an original iron-lace side panel. It puts the city's hand-made civic design on court. Pitch it for 2027-28, since the 2026-27 jersey is presumably locked already (its design is unverified). Back-plan it so concept, Pelicans sign-off and NBA approval land in the league's next submission window. Meanwhile, run its tile and iron-lace language on 2026-27 lifestyle product.
motifs: Square-tile block capitals set on a grid, with a tile border around the wordmark
Original iron-lace railing drawing with a hidden 'NO' monogram in the scrollwork
Pelican in her piety, the state's comeback bird, inside the collar
uniform.typography: A 'NEW ORLEANS' wordmark and numbers built square by square on a tile grid, in glazed-white fills with a thin navy outline on cobalt. A paid New Orleans sign painter draws and signs them. No script and no fleur-de-lis in the wordmark.
details: Base: cobalt, for clear contrast with the white Association set and the navy Icon set
Waistband: ward numerals in tile type running around the band, plus WESTBANK and THE EAST
Side panel: tonal iron-lace jacquard in a deeper cobalt, with the monogram at hip height
Jock tag: debossed brass crescent-and-star roundel with the lettering artist's signature
Court: tile-bordered street-name corners at each baseline, as if the court sits on a city corner
avoid: Purple, green and gold as the lead. It's tourist shorthand and blurs into LSU, and the team's fan-favorite purple-and-neon NOLA Nights set already owns purple.
Fleur-de-lis as the hero. It reads as the Saints and as souvenir shorthand, and the Pelicans mark already carries one. Its history in colonial Louisiana is a secondary reason for restraint.
Black Masking Indian beadwork, plumes or chief iconography in any form, and copying any club's regalia
Katrina waterlines, FEMA X-codes, voodoo and Bourbon Street or 'N'awlins' tourist shorthand
Copying a real tiled street name, a specific building's railing, or Simon's or Dr. Bob's signature styles

alternates.name: Sousaphone
alternates.idea: Navy with brushed Pelicans Gold as brass, and numbers in drum-head sign-painter lettering. Co-designed with a credited brass band and paired with school instrument donations.

alternates.name: Streetcar
alternates.idea: St. Charles streetcar olive green with gold roller-sign numerals and iron-lace side panels, a quiet fall alternate.

calendar.window: League tip-off, Oct 20 to Oct 30, before the Cup opener at the Clippers. The Pelicans' own opener date is still to confirm.
calendar.moment: Mosley's debut and the season's optimism peak
calendar.play: Seed Corner Tile tees and snapbacks in the arena and online, with 'still here' player tees for confirmed Nike names. Hold Ward Call's arena launch for the first confirmed home date.

calendar.window: First confirmed home game after Oct 30, then confirmed Cup Friday home nights through Nov 27
calendar.moment: NBA Cup West Group B (OKC, MIN, LAC, MEM) and phase one of Ward Call
calendar.play: Launch Ward Call with three areas and a paid bounce lineup led by Katey Red, Sissy Nobby and DJ Jubilee. Use one Friday-night-in-New-Orleans giveaway graphic for any Cup opponent at home.

calendar.moment: Southern vs. Grambling at the Superdome (game Saturday Nov 28) with the Battle of the Bands on Black Friday, also the last Cup Friday
calendar.play: Drop a licensed HBCU-coded capsule with Southern and Grambling's programs, sized to whether the Pelicans are home that night. Leave the tailgate lots to the schools.
calendar.channel: Arena store and digital, with a pop-up only if the Pelicans are home

calendar.moment: Holiday gifting, the year's biggest retail peak (no Christmas Day game)
calendar.play: Push value kids and ward bundles, the 'Piety' warm-up as a premium gift and the full Ward Call set. Launch the brass series at a December home game.

calendar.moment: King cake season and the start of Carnival
calendar.play: Drop the Twelfth Night Pack with a doubloon jock-tag hunt, and give away paid Dong Phuong king cake slices at a Carnival-season home night.
calendar.channel: Arena, Fleurty Girl and Dirty Coast doors, and digital

calendar.window: Around Feb 6, Tết in New Orleans East
calendar.moment: Vietnamese New Orleans' biggest gathering, inside Carnival
calendar.play: No product. Pay Vietnamese New Orleanian artists to design a Pelicans game-night element and ask the community whether product is wanted at all.

calendar.window: Feb 10 to early March: after Mardi Gras, through the trade deadline, All-Star and the LHSAA playoffs
calendar.moment: Post-Carnival reset, when basketball and school pride get the city back
calendar.play: Run city-only rapid-response tees with Dirty Coast and Fleurty Girl, with no player names or likenesses. Restock Ward Call, send out the brass second wave, and hold a school-pride Friday home night with one partner program.
calendar.channel: Local brand doors, arena and digital

calendar.window: Late February through Apr 16 (Lent, crawfish, any Play-In)
calendar.moment: Crawfish season and the stretch run. The March Super Sundays and St. Joseph's Night are no-brand zones.
calendar.play: Launch Boil Season around confirmed home dates, and print a Play-In tee only if the team qualifies. Stay away from Super Sunday weekends and Mar 19 entirely.

calendar.channel: Magazine Street, festival-season pop-ups and digital

partners.name: Dirty Coast
partners.why: Its neighborhood in-jokes are what locals wear over team gear, the city-first voice the Pelicans lack.
partners.idea: Paid co-designer of Ward Call copy and of city-only rapid-response tees with no player names or likenesses.

partners.name: Fleurty Girl
partners.type: Local tee and gift brand (French Quarter, Lakeside Metairie and Gretna doors)
partners.why: It became the local face of the city's tee vernacular when the NFL sent its 2010 'Who Dat' letters. It reaches local women and families on both sides of the river.
partners.idea: Host the Twelfth Night drop in its doors and co-design a family and kids Carnival tee.

partners.name: Bounce artists (Katey Red, Sissy Nobby, DJ Jubilee; Big Freedia once cleared)
partners.type: Rotating paid lineup of bounce pioneers and DJs
partners.why: The ward-by-ward call-and-response is the city's most local typography, and credit belongs to the group that built it, not one headliner.
partners.idea: Paid arena sets for Ward Call launches and the Decadence-weekend night, with names on hangtags and the scoreboard.

partners.name: Xavier, Dillard, Southern and Grambling
partners.type: HBCUs and their licensing and band programs
partners.why: HBCU pride peaks on Bayou Classic weekend, and Xavier and Dillard are the city's own Black college communities.
partners.idea: Licensed HBCU-night capsule with proceeds and band support returned through each school's program.

partners.name: Studio BE (Brandan 'BMike' Odums)
partners.why: The city's most credible street artist. His work paints back what was lost after Katrina and urban renewal.
partners.idea: An invitation, which he can decline, to own the Claiborne Oaks capsule and choose its beneficiary.

partners.name: Rebirth Brass Band with the Tipitina's Foundation
partners.type: Brass band and school music nonprofit
partners.why: Rebirth is the standard every second-line band is measured against, and the foundation equips school band programs.
partners.idea: Once members' deals are checked, credit Rebirth on the first brass-series drop and fund instruments for every unit sold.

partners.name: Dong Phuong Bakery
partners.why: Its king cake draws lines from every corner of the metro, and it carries both the Carnival and Vietnamese New Orleans stories.
partners.idea: Paid supplier of king cake for an in-arena Carnival-night giveaway and a named food partner for a Tết game-night element.

partners.name: Backstreet Cultural Museum
partners.type: Community museum of second-line and Black Masking culture, Tremé
partners.why: It knows who to ask, but it is one advisor, not a gatekeeper for every club or tribe.
partners.idea: A paid advisor on the Second Line Sunday pilot who names who else belongs at the table. Consent comes from each club and band directly.

where: Taste: Dirty Coast on Magazine Street, Fleurty Girl's French Quarter, Metairie and Gretna doors, St. Claude pop-ups and Studio BE, where limited drops land first.
Volume: Lakeside (Metairie) and Oakwood (Gretna) mall doors and Dick's, where families buy kids jerseys and mainstream colorways.
Launch: the Pelicans Team Store at Smoothie King Center for Ward Call, Twelfth Night and school and HBCU nights.
Regional: a Gulf South line (ward-free 'Louisiana' and 'Gulf South' tile pieces) sold in Baton Rouge, Acadiana and Gulf Coast doors and online for fans outside the metro.
when: Late October to December is peak Pelicans attention and the year's biggest gifting window.
Jan 6 to about Jan 26 for Carnival product; no hero launch in the two weeks before Mardi Gras (Feb 9).
School-pride and visitor drops: Bayou Classic on Thanksgiving weekend, the LHSAA playoffs from February to early March, and Essence on July 4 weekend.
Late February through Jazz Fest for the lightweight stretch-run and festival palette.
how: Plan about two-thirds of units as city-first product with a secondary Pelicans mark and one-third as player and team product.
Tier the range: value kids, tee and swingman bundles for local households, and numbered keepsake pieces for visitors. Set separate sell-through targets per tier.
Design for 60-80°F parade days and air-conditioned arenas: mesh, seersucker, packable shells and color-matchable tonal sets.
Pay and credit every collaborator up front, and send money back where people can see it: instruments, school programs, corridor groups. This market checks.

risks.risk: Cultural extraction would end Nike's credibility with the communities that set the city's style. That means anything resembling Black Masking Indian beadwork, or an unpaid second-line reference.
risks.mitigation: Keep sacred material out of every brief, pay culture bearers up front, and get written consent from each club, band and artist directly.

risks.risk: Player product depends on deals Nike may not hold: Zion is a Jordan Brand athlete with a long injury history, and Murphy, Queen and Fears' apparel arrangements are unconfirmed.
risks.mitigation: Confirm each player's arrangement before assigning product, run Zion pieces through Jordan Brand, and lead with city and ward product where deals are unclear.

risks.risk: Another sub-30-win season or a Murphy trade at the Feb 11 deadline could crater team-gear demand and feed fan worry about the team's permanence.
risks.mitigation: Hold team-branded volume to about a third, keep rapid-response tees city-only, and tell 'still here' stories rather than contention.

risks.risk: Third-party IP is everywhere: Saints fleur-de-lis treatments, 'Who Dat', krewe marks, HBCU and high school marks, and the King Cake Baby. There are also NBA and NBPA player rights, and Hornets-era marks owned by Charlotte. Some school marks are tied to other brands and involve minors.
risks.mitigation: Use original commissioned art, route school and HBCU work through each institution's licensing office, clear the King Cake Baby with the Pelicans, and keep local-brand tees free of player likenesses.

risks.risk: Unknown 2026-27 home dates could put launches on road nights. Hurricane season (June 1 to Nov 30) can wipe out summer and early-fall events. And Aug 29 is a day of grief.
risks.mitigation: Pin every in-arena launch to a confirmed home date, keep digital fallbacks, and schedule nothing commercial around Aug 29.

scorecard.rationale: The starkest split in the league: New Orleans's culture is second only to New York's, but thin retail, a Saints-first city and a 26-56 team put opportunity, retail and fandom at the floor. It's a craft market, not a volume market (brief scores: opportunity 46, culture 96, retail 34, fandom 38). Few NBA cities have a deeper or more design-ready local culture, and its calendar lines up with the season. But retail is thin: few destination sneaker doors, a modest arena store and a price-conscious core. Pelicans fandom is small, Saints-first and weary after 26-56. The opportunity sits just below average, held up by city-first product that can sell regardless of the standings.

music.headline: New Orleans music runs on a street calendar, with the Pelicans' October-to-June hours
music.summary: Jazz was born here, and the city's living sounds are just as homegrown: Tremé brass bands like Rebirth, Sunday second lines, Black Masking Indian chants and bounce. Cash Money and No Limit turned Uptown housing developments into global brands. Locals police hometown loyalty hard, so a rebuilding Pelicans team should sound like the city by paying the clubs, bands and bounce artists who make it.

insights.title: Second-line Sundays run on the NBA clock
insights.detail: Social Aid & Pleasure Clubs such as Young Men Olympian Jr. (1884), Prince of Wales and Black Men of Labor parade most Sundays from around Labor Day into June. Each club marches behind a hired brass band in a new matching suit, sash and fan scheme, kept secret until parade day. The season tracks the Pelicans' October-to-April schedule almost exactly.
insights.implication: Build Sunday home games and drops around the second line. Each season, pay one club to co-design a colorway. Pay its band too, and cover the club's police and permit fees. Don't stage a branded "second line" for content.

insights.title: Bounce is the city's own hip-hop dialect
insights.detail: Bounce grew out of early-'90s project and block parties on the Triggerman beat, sampled from the Showboys' "Drag Rap." Its chants shout out wards and housing developments, as in MC T. Tucker and DJ Irv's 1991 "Where Dey At." Big Freedia, Katey Red and Sissy Nobby carried it through Katrina. Freedia took it worldwide. Her voice is on Beyoncé's "Formation" and "Break My Soul" and on Drake's "Nice for What."
insights.implication: A call-and-response, ward-by-ward type system across all 17 wards is the most local typography the city offers. Launch it with bounce artists and credit the queer artists who built the genre. Drop the dated "sissy bounce" label.

insights.title: Cash Money and No Limit made Uptown a global brand
insights.detail: Master P's No Limit (Calliope) and Birdman and Slim Williams' Cash Money set the late-'90s Southern rap template. Cash Money ran from Magnolia to Hollygrove. The sound had Mannie Fresh's 808 production, Juvenile's "Back That Azz Up," B.G.'s "Bling Bling" and Lil Wayne's rise. Peaches Records sold it, and Pen & Pixel's chrome-and-gold covers packaged it. Juvenile's NPR Tiny Desk set with Mannie Fresh shows the catalog still lands nationally.
insights.implication: That Y2K chrome-and-diamond look matches the franchise's 2002 arrival in New Orleans, so it makes an honest nostalgia lane for a throwback capsule. Label marks, cover art and song titles need licensing and the artists' participation.

insights.title: Brass is the city's real arena sound
insights.detail: Tremé produced the modern brass-band explosion. Philip and Keith Frazier founded Rebirth Brass Band in 1983 at Joseph S. Clark High, with Kermit Ruffins. Rebirth still holds Tuesday nights at the Maple Leaf. Rebirth snare drummer Derrick Tabb's The Roots of Music and the Tipitina's Foundation keep school band programs equipped. Pelicans Gold (#85714D) already looks like a tarnished sousaphone bell.
insights.implication: Make brass the material and type story: brushed-brass foil and hardware, bass-drum-head lettering, and launches led by a working brass band. Pair each with an instrument donation to a school band program.

insights.title: Carnival and HBCU bands are the city's stadium sound
insights.detail: St. Augustine's Marching 100, the Seventh Ward Purple Knights, became the first Black band in the Rex parade in 1967. They headline Carnival alongside Edna Karr, Warren Easton and other high-school bands. On Thanksgiving weekend, the Bayou Classic Battle of the Bands (Southern's Human Jukebox vs. Grambling's World Famed Tiger Marching Band) fills the Superdome next door to the Smoothie King Center.
insights.implication: Band-uniform details (frogging, epaulets, cross-belts, plumes) give warm-ups and shooting shirts a credible look for a Mardi Gras-week or Bayou Classic-weekend drop. Co-create it with a band program, and pay the band back in uniforms or instruments.

insights.title: Hometown-first is the loyalty test
insights.detail: The NFL picked Kendrick Lamar over Lil Wayne to headline Super Bowl LIX at the Superdome in February 2025. Wayne said publicly that the snub hurt, and locals took it personally, even though Jon Batiste sang the anthem and Trombone Shorty played the pregame. New Orleans judges brands by whether its own artists lead. A rebuilding Pelicans team faces the same test: Zion Williamson, Trey Murphy III, Derik Queen and Jeremiah Fears, under first-year coach Jamahl Mosley.
insights.implication: Front every Pelicans music collaboration with New Orleans talent from bounce, brass or Uptown rap. A national guest can feature but never headline. Clear every artist's footwear and apparel deals before outreach.

places.name: Congo Square (Louis Armstrong Park)
places.why: Enslaved and free Africans gathered here on Sundays in the 18th and 19th centuries to drum and dance. It is the root of the city's rhythm and the namesake of Jazz Fest's Congo Square stage.

places.name: Maple Leaf Bar
places.why: Rebirth Brass Band's decades-long Tuesday-night residency is the city's most dependable brass ritual.

places.name: Tipitina's
places.why: Professor Longhair's namesake room has belonged to the band Galactic since 2018. Its foundation supplies instruments to school bands.

places.name: Kermit's Treme Mother-in-Law Lounge
places.why: Ernie K-Doe's mural-covered shrine, now run by trumpeter Kermit Ruffins, is a neighborhood-scale room for brass and trad jazz under the Claiborne overpass.

places.name: Preservation Hall
places.why: The keeper of traditional New Orleans jazz since 1961, and home of the Preservation Hall Jazz Band, led by Ben Jaffe.

places.name: Peaches Records
places.why: Shirani "Peaches" Rea's shop sold early bounce and Cash Money and No Limit tapes. It remains a hub for local rap and bounce.

places.name: Louisiana Music Factory
places.why: The deepest stock of local music in the city, with in-store sets during festival season.

places.name: WWOZ 90.7 FM
places.why: The listener-supported jazz and heritage station posts the weekly second-line schedule and broadcasts Jazz Fest. It also carries tastemaker shows such as DJ Soul Sister's.

places.name: Dew Drop Inn
places.why: The Chitlin' Circuit hub where Little Richard, Allen Toussaint and Irma Thomas played reopened in 2023 as a hotel and music lounge.

places.name: Q93 (WQUE 93.3 FM)
places.why: The city's hip-hop station breaks local rap and bounce records. It is the mainstream outlet for any Pelicans-linked music drop.

people.name: Big Freedia
people.why: The genre's global face, through Beyoncé's "Formation" and "Break My Soul" and Drake's "Nice for What." The natural lead for any bounce-rooted Pelicans launch.

people.name: Juvenile
people.why: "Back That Azz Up," produced by Mannie Fresh, is the city's party anthem. His NPR Tiny Desk set with Mannie Fresh renewed his national reach.

people.name: Lil Wayne
people.why: The city's biggest rap star. His Super Bowl LIX snub made him a symbol of hometown loyalty.

people.name: Trombone Shorty (Troy Andrews)
people.why: A regular Jazz Fest closer who hosts the Treme Threauxdown and runs a foundation and academy for young musicians. That makes him a credible youth-music partner.

people.name: Rebirth Brass Band
people.why: The band that modernized brass with funk and hip-hop, and the standard every second-line band is measured against.

people.name: Jon Batiste
people.why: A Grammy Album of the Year winner who sang the anthem at Super Bowl LIX in the Superdome. He bridges the city's jazz lineage and mainstream pop.

people.name: Tank and the Bangas
people.role: Soul, funk and spoken-word band led by Tarriona 'Tank' Ball
people.why: Winners of NPR's 2017 Tiny Desk Contest and 2020 Best New Artist Grammy nominees, with a playful, colorful visual identity suited to co-designed product.

people.name: Rob49
people.why: The rising street-rap name of the 2020s, through his "Vulture Island" mixtapes and hits like "On Dat Money." Younger fans now rep him.

moments.name: Second-line season
moments.timing: Most Sundays, from around Labor Day into June
moments.why: Social Aid & Pleasure Club parades with brass bands run through the entire NBA season. They give the city a weekly street ritual to align Sunday home games and drops with.

moments.name: Bayou Classic Battle of the Bands
moments.why: Southern's Human Jukebox and Grambling's Tiger Marching Band face off next door to the Smoothie King Center. It is the biggest HBCU band moment of the year.

moments.name: Mardi Gras (Carnival parade season)
moments.timing: Late January through Fat Tuesday, Feb 9, 2027
moments.why: High-school marching bands like St. Augustine's Marching 100 are the parades' real headliners, and the whole city is outside in purple, green and gold.

moments.name: Super Sunday and St. Joseph's Night
moments.why: Black Masking Indian tribes come out in new hand-sewn suits, with chants and drums. It is a sacred community event to respect, not a brand stage.

moments.name: French Quarter Festival
moments.why: A free, locals-heavy festival of hometown acts, it lands as the regular season ends.

moments.name: New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival
moments.timing: Last weekend of April and first weekend of May, Fair Grounds Race Course
moments.why: The city's biggest music event overlaps the first round of the playoffs and pulls the national music press to town.

moments.name: Essence Festival of Culture
moments.why: The country's largest Black music and culture festival keeps New Orleans in the national conversation through the offseason and Summer League.

moments.name: Satchmo SummerFest
moments.timing: Early August, around Louis Armstrong's Aug 4 birthday
moments.why: A hometown tribute to Armstrong at the Old U.S. Mint that bridges the offseason to second-line season.

vocabulary.meaning: The crowd that follows a club and its brass band (the "main line") through the streets. Also the Sunday parade itself, and the dance.
The high-energy, improvised footwork of the second line. It's also the root of the Lady and Men Buckjumpers club name.
Bounce's signature call-and-response, answered by shouting your ward or neighborhood. It comes from MC T. Tucker and DJ Irv's 1991 record.
The looped drum break, from the Showboys' "Drag Rap," that sits under nearly every bounce record.
One of the city's 17 political districts. "What ward you from?" is a core identity question and the backbone of bounce shout-outs (Seventh Ward, Ninth Ward, 17th Ward).
Close friend or partner, popularized nationally by Cash Money-era New Orleans rap.
Flashy jewelry and shine. It was coined on B.G.'s 1999 Cash Money single and later added to the Oxford English Dictionary.
The sacred hymn that opens and closes Black Masking Indian gatherings. Recognize it, and never use it in marketing.

designCues.cue: Pelicans Gold treated as sousaphone brass: brushed-brass foil, metal aglets and zipper pulls in Pelicans Gold against Pelicans Navy (#0C2340).
designCues.source: The worn horns of Tremé brass bands, especially the sousaphone bell that leads every second line.
designCues.use: Foil, embroidery thread and hardware on a brass-themed capsule. Tie the story to a named working band, not generic "jazz."

designCues.cue: Bass-drum-head lettering: band name arched across the top of a circle, city or year across the bottom, in sign-painter script with outlines and drop shadows.
designCues.source: The hand-painted bass drum heads carried by Rebirth, TBC and other brass bands on the street.
designCues.use: A circular "drum head" lockup for chest graphics, patches and hangtags. Commission a New Orleans sign painter, and never copy an existing band's drum.

designCues.cue: Parade-day regalia: satin, sequins, rhinestones, ostrich-plume fans, streamers and decorated umbrellas in a club's coordinated colors.
designCues.source: Social Aid & Pleasure Club sashes, fans and umbrellas, made by members for each year's parade.
designCues.use: Satin taping, sequin patches and a printed second-line handkerchief for a limited Sunday capsule. Commission them from the club members who make the regalia.

designCues.cue: The annual color reveal: each club keeps its new suit colors secret until it steps out of the hall on parade day.
designCues.source: Social Aid & Pleasure Club parade tradition.
designCues.use: Launch a capsule or City Edition as a parade-day reveal with a partner club, not a leak-then-drop rollout.

designCues.cue: Call-and-response type: stacked shout-outs in tall condensed caps, one ward per line ("WHERE DEY AT?" then "SEVENTH WARD").
designCues.source: Bounce chants that call out wards and neighborhoods.
designCues.use: Ward-by-ward tees and shooting shirts, co-written with bounce artists. Use ward numbers, not the names of demolished housing projects, unless artists from those communities lead.

designCues.cue: Y2K chrome: beveled chrome and gold 3D type, diamonds, flames and stacked photo collage.
designCues.source: Pen & Pixel Graphics' late-'90s album covers for No Limit and Cash Money.
designCues.use: A reference for a 2002-era throwback capsule. Commission original art, and license any label marks or cover references.

designCues.cue: Marching-band silhouette: frogging, epaulets, cross-belts and plumed-shako proportions.
designCues.source: St. Augustine's Marching 100 and the high-school and HBCU bands of Carnival and the Bayou Classic.
designCues.use: A warm-up jacket and shooting shirt with braid and frogging trim for Mardi Gras week or Bayou Classic weekend, co-created with a band program.

designCues.cue: Carnival purple, the shade locals wait for on the parade route when the Purple Knights' band comes into view.
designCues.source: Rex's 1872 purple, green and gold, and St. Augustine's purple-and-gold Marching 100.
designCues.use: An accent with Pelicans Navy and Gold on a Mardi Gras-week drop. Skip literal beads, masks and jester clichés.

productHooks: "Second Line Sunday" capsule: a satin-trimmed warm-up, printed handkerchief and drum-head tee in a colorway co-designed with one Social Aid & Pleasure Club. Reveal it parade-style before a Sunday home game, with proceeds covering the club's parade fees.
"Where Dey At" ward pack: 17 ward tees and a shooting shirt in bounce call-and-response type. Big Freedia or another bounce artist launches it with an in-arena bounce set.

Brass series: Pelicans Gold foil-and-hardware hoodies and tees. Credit each drop to a named brass band (Rebirth first), and pair it with an instrument donation through the Tipitina's Foundation or The Roots of Music.

Marching-band warm-up for Mardi Gras week and Bayou Classic weekend: a frogging-trimmed jacket in Carnival purple, Pelicans Navy and Gold, co-created with St. Augustine's Marching 100 or another band program.
Jazz Fest-window playoff tee: a poster-style print commissioned from a Black New Orleans artist, dropped when the festival overlaps the first round. Use no Jazz Fest marks without a license.
watchouts: Black Masking (Mardi Gras) Indian suits, beaded patches, chants such as "Indian Red" and Big Chiefs' names are sacred and individually authored. Never reproduce or sample them. Commission, credit and pay only masking artists who choose to take part.
Bounce was built by queer artists (Big Freedia, Katey Red, Sissy Nobby). Credit and pay them, don't use the culture as edgy flavor, and avoid the dated "sissy bounce" tag.
Songs like "Back That Azz Up" and "Iko Iko," the Cash Money and No Limit label marks, Pen & Pixel art, and the Jazz Fest, Tipitina's and Preservation Hall names are third-party IP. License them.

Second lines are working-class Black neighborhood institutions, under pressure from gentrification, permit costs and past violence on parade routes. Stage no branded second lines, take no parade photos without the clubs' consent, and pay bands fairly.

Housing-project names (Magnolia, Calliope, Lafitte, St. Bernard, Desire) recall public housing demolished after Katrina and residents displaced. Use them only when artists from those communities lead, and clear each artist's footwear and apparel contracts before outreach.

art.headline: New Orleans looks hand-made, and no jersey has borrowed its handwriting yet
art.summary: Iron lace, tile street names and hand-painted signs give the city its look. Its street art paints back what was taken, from BMike Odums in abandoned housing developments to the live oaks on the I-10 columns. The 2023-24 fan-favorite City Edition, brought back in 2025-26, showed that locals reward city color over team color. The next step is commissioned craft, not more fleur-de-lis.

insights.title: Carnival is two visual systems, not one
insights.detail: Old-line krewes speak in gilded papier-mâché floats, flambeaux and aluminum doubloons, which Rex introduced in 1960. Their colors are the purple, green and gold Rex chose in 1872. Black street Carnival speaks in Black Masking Indian beadwork, Baby Doll satin bonnets and, at dawn in Tremé, the North Side Skull and Bone Gang's papier-mâché skulls.
insights.implication: The krewe palette is already on the fan-favorite City Edition, so repeating it adds little. The untapped layer is craft. Black street Carnival can enter product only through named, paid collaborators, never as surface pattern.

insights.title: The defining walls are under the interstate and inside abandoned buildings
insights.detail: The I-10 overpass built over Claiborne Avenue in the late 1960s erased the oak-lined neutral ground at the heart of Black Tremé. Its columns are now painted with oaks, Indians and neighborhood history, and Indians and families gather there on Mardi Gras Day. BMike Odums built his name painting the abandoned Florida housing development (the Project Be and Exhibit Be shows) and Algiers' DeGaulle Manor. Then he opened Studio BE in Bywater.
insights.implication: New Orleans street art paints back what Katrina and urban renewal took. Commission Tremé, Seventh Ward and Ninth Ward artists for new work in that spirit. Don't reproduce existing murals.

insights.title: The city's lettering is hand-painted and tile-set
insights.detail: Street names are spelled in blue-and-white tile at sidewalk corners. Simon of New Orleans' dot-bordered, glittered signs hang in bars and restaurants citywide. Dr. Bob's "Be Nice or Leave" signs are painted on found wood and framed in bottle caps. Sno-ball stands and corner stores still hand-letter their menus.
insights.implication: Generic sports script could be from anywhere. A commissioned hand-lettered alphabet and tile-set numerals would read as New Orleans at a glance, on jerseys, warm-ups and retail graphics.

insights.title: The fleur-de-lis is a trap, and the city defends its symbols
insights.detail: The fleur-de-lis reads as the Saints. Louisiana's 1724 Code Noir also ordered recaptured runaway enslaved people branded with it. In 2010 the NFL sent cease-and-desist letters to local shops such as Fleurty Girl over "Who Dat" shirts. The backlash from fans and state officials made the league back off.
insights.implication: Lead with other cues. Never try to claim a local phrase as Nike or NBA property, and treat local tee makers as partners, not infringers.

insights.title: Status is earned by hand
insights.detail: Big Chiefs spend most of a year sewing suits from tens of thousands of beads, rhinestones and plumes, competing to be the "prettiest." Demond Melancon's beadwork now hangs in museums and galleries. Social Aid & Pleasure Clubs debut new suits, sashes and decorated umbrellas each parade. Krewe of Red Beans members glue bean mosaics onto suits.
insights.implication: Hand-finished, numbered, artist-signed pieces carry more local prestige than any print. Build the top tier of a New Orleans collection around makers' handwork, and pay and credit the makers.

insights.title: A Carnival fabrication bench works year-round
insights.detail: Kern Studios, whose Mardi Gras World warehouses sit on the riverfront, and independent float builders sculpt foam, papier-mâché and gold leaf all year. When COVID canceled the 2021 parades, Devin De Wulf's Hire a Mardi Gras Artist paid out-of-work float artists to turn homes into "house floats."
insights.implication: Commission float artists for Smoothie King Center installations, retail fixtures and a Carnival-season pop-up. The same hands that build the parades should build the launch.

places.name: Studio BE
places.why: BMike Odums's warehouse of monumental spray-painted portraits and text pieces is the city's best-known contemporary street-art space. It is also the clearest route to a credible collaborator.

places.name: Claiborne Avenue overpass columns ('under the bridge')
places.neighborhood: Tremé / Seventh Ward (N. Claiborne Ave under I-10)
places.why: Columns painted with live oaks and Black New Orleans history stand where the neutral ground was lost. On Mardi Gras Day they frame the city's most important street gathering.

places.name: St. Claude Arts District
places.neighborhood: Marigny / St. Roch / Bywater (St. Claude Ave)
places.why: Artist-run spaces such as The Front and Good Children Gallery hold Second Saturday openings. This is the scene's experimental, emerging-artist end.

places.name: Julia Street Arts District
places.why: Established galleries such as Arthur Roger Gallery and Jonathan Ferrara Gallery represent the city's major painters. They host White Linen Night and Art for Art's Sake.

places.name: Ogden Museum of Southern Art
places.neighborhood: Warehouse District (Camp St at Lee Circle)
places.why: The deepest collection of Southern art and self-taught work, with Thursday-night Ogden After Hours concerts that draw a local creative crowd.

places.name: Ashé Cultural Arts Center
places.why: Founded by Carol Bebelle and Douglas Redd, it anchors Black visual art and Indian and second-line culture on the boulevard. It is a natural co-host for community-led product.

places.name: Mardi Gras World (Kern Studios)
places.neighborhood: Riverfront by the Convention Center (Port of New Orleans Place)
places.why: The warehouses where Carnival floats are sculpted, painted and gilded hold the city's largest commercial fabrication talent pool.

places.name: Music Box Village
places.neighborhood: Bywater (N. Rampart St near the Industrial Canal)
places.why: New Orleans Airlift's playable houses, built from salvage, show the city's make-it-from-what's-left design ethic. They host concerts and fabrication.

places.name: The Historic New Orleans Collection
places.neighborhood: French Quarter (Royal St and Chartres St)
places.why: The best archive of the city's maps, Carnival design drawings, signage and ironwork. Designers should research here before drawing anything.

places.name: Xavier University of Louisiana, Department of Art
places.why: MacArthur Fellow sculptor John T. Scott taught here for four decades. It remains a pipeline for Black New Orleans artists and designers.

people.name: Brandan 'BMike' Odums
people.role: Painter, muralist and filmmaker; founder of Studio BE
people.why: His large spray-painted portraits of civil-rights and local figures were born in Project Be and Exhibit Be. He is the most credible New Orleans street artist for a City Edition or Black history collaboration.

people.name: Demond Melancon
people.role: Big Chief of the Young Seminole Hunters; beadwork artist
people.why: His hand-beaded suits and portrait panels cross from the street to museums. He is the model for a paid, credited, maker-led beadwork commission.

people.name: Willie Birch
people.role: Painter and sculptor of Seventh Ward life
people.why: His large black-and-white drawings of second lines, porches and neighbors are the elder-statesman record of the Seventh Ward. A tribute or commission would carry real weight there.

people.name: Bruce Davenport Jr.
people.role: Lower Ninth Ward artist known for marker drawings of marching bands
people.why: His dense, colorful drawings of high-school marching bands bridge New Orleans' band culture and sports spectacle. A natural fit for game-night and youth product.

people.name: Simon of New Orleans (Simon Hardeveld)
people.why: His bright, dot-bordered, glittered signs, signed "Simon," hang all over the city and define its hand-lettered look.

people.name: Dr. Bob (Bob Shaffer)
people.why: His "Be Nice or Leave" signs on salvaged wood framed in bottle caps are the city's most recognized hand-painted phrase.

people.name: L. Kasimu Harris
people.why: His series on vanishing Black bars and lounges documents Black New Orleans social life from inside. He is a credible lens for campaigns and product stories.

people.name: Fleurty Girl (Lauren Haydel)
people.why: A target of the NFL's 2010 "Who Dat" cease-and-desist letters, it is the local face of the city's own fan-tee vernacular. It is a natural rapid-response partner.

moments.name: Twelfth Night opens Carnival
moments.timing: January 6 (Joan of Arc parade in the French Quarter; Phunny Phorty Phellows ride the St. Charles streetcar)
moments.why: The city switches into Carnival look and color for six weeks. It is the natural launch for a Carnival-season drop.

moments.name: Lundi Gras and Mardi Gras Day
moments.why: Krewe of Red Beans bean suits come out on Lundi Gras. Then Zulu, Rex, Indians, Baby Dolls and the Skull and Bone Gang take over on the day. It is the year's peak of street costume and craft.

moments.name: Uptown Super Sunday
moments.timing: Sunday near St. Joseph's Day (March 19), traditionally from A.L. Davis Park in Central City
moments.why: Black Masking Indian tribes show their suits in daylight. This is the moment to meet chiefs about commissions, as guests and never as a marketing backdrop.

moments.name: Jazz Fest and its posters
moments.timing: Last weekend of April and first weekend of May
moments.why: The official Jazz Fest and Congo Square silkscreen posters are a decades-old collector tradition. They prove New Orleanians buy numbered local art prints.

moments.name: White Linen Night
moments.timing: First Saturday of August, Julia Street
moments.why: The Warehouse District's summer gallery night is an offseason stage for an artist reveal before the season starts.

moments.name: Art for Art's Sake
moments.timing: First Saturday of October, Julia Street and Magazine Street
moments.why: The gallery season opener lands weeks before tip-off. It is a ready-made unveiling for City Edition art or an artist-in-residence.

moments.name: Second-line Sundays
moments.timing: Most Sundays, roughly late August through June
moments.why: Social Aid & Pleasure Clubs parade in new coordinated suits, sashes and umbrellas each year. It is the city's living fashion show.

moments.name: Monthly gallery nights
moments.timing: Second Saturday on St. Claude Ave; first Saturday on Julia St
moments.why: The standing circuit for scouting artists and for small-run, artist-credited drops.

vocabulary.meaning: A covered porch or upper porch held up by posts from the street. Locals and preservationists distinguish it from a cantilevered balcony.
The ornamental cast and wrought iron on French Quarter and Garden District galleries and fences, such as the Pontalba "AP" railings and the Cornstalk fence on Royal St.
A Carnival organization that parades or holds a ball. Now used for any crew with a shared purpose.
What riders toss from floats: beads, cups, doubloons and coveted hand-decorated pieces such as Zulu coconuts and Muses shoes.
Making and wearing a costume. To "mask Indian" means sewing and wearing a suit as a Black Masking Indian, a year-long commitment.
The crowd that dances behind a club and its brass band (the "main line") in a Sunday parade or jazz funeral.
The median of a boulevard, where families stake out parade spots and where Claiborne's lost oaks once stood.
A little something extra, given free. A natural name for a hidden inside-the-collar or jock-tag detail.

designCues.cue: Sidewalk-tile cobalt (approx. #1E4D9B) on glazed white (approx. #F3F0E6). Set it as square-tile block capitals with a tile border.
designCues.source: The tiled street names inlaid at sidewalk corners across the French Quarter, Marigny and Uptown.
designCues.use: Numbers, neighborhood names (TREMÉ, ST. CLAUDE, CENTRAL CITY) and a "NEW ORLEANS" wordmark built tile by tile. No other city has a typographic system like it.

designCues.cue: St. Charles streetcar green, a dark olive (approx. #3F5B37; match to the RTA paint), trimmed with gold numerals.
designCues.source: The 1923-24 Perley Thomas cars still running on the St. Charles line, the world's oldest continuously operating street railway.
designCues.use: A fall lifestyle base or alternate colorway with Pelicans gold numerals. The roller-sign destination type can inspire secondary lettering.

designCues.cue: Iron lace: repeating cast-iron gallery railing with a monogram hidden in the scrollwork.
designCues.source: The Pontalba Buildings' railings on Jackson Square, with the Baroness de Pontalba's "AP" cast in, and French Quarter galleries and fences.
designCues.use: Laser-cut perforations, jacquard knits and shorts side panels with a "NO" or Pelicans monogram woven into an original railing drawing. Don't copy a specific building.

designCues.cue: Hand-painted sign lettering: bright caps outlined in dots, glitter fills and found-wood borders.
designCues.source: Simon of New Orleans' glittered signs, Dr. Bob's bottle-cap-framed "Be Nice or Leave" and hand-lettered sno-ball stand menus.
designCues.use: Commission a New Orleans sign painter to hand-letter an original "PELICANS" / "NEW ORLEANS" alphabet for lifestyle graphics, signed and credited. Never imitate Simon's or Dr. Bob's signature style without them.

designCues.cue: Crescent moon and stars inside a cast-iron circle.
designCues.source: The city's cast-iron water meter covers. Their crescent-and-star motif nods to the "Crescent City" nickname and is already a beloved rubbing and print subject.
designCues.use: A debossed jock tag, outsole or patch icon. A quiet "Crescent City" mark for locals that avoids the fleur-de-lis.

designCues.cue: The doubloon: a coin with the krewe emblem on one face and the year's theme on the other, struck in anodized aluminum (purple, green and gold among many colors).
designCues.source: Doubloons, introduced by Rex in 1960, are the throw every Carnival kid scrambles for.
designCues.use: Two-sided metal jock tags, hang tags and limited Pelicans doubloons with a new theme each season. Make them with or license them from a doubloon maker, and never copy a krewe's emblem.

designCues.cue: Second-line regalia: satin sashes, ribbon fringe, sequins and feather-trimmed umbrellas in each club's color of the year.
designCues.source: Social Aid & Pleasure Clubs such as Black Men of Labor, Lady Buckjumpers and Prince of Wales, which reveal new outfits on parade day.
designCues.use: Satin and fringe trims for a fan-wear capsule made with a named club. The club picks the colors, gets paid and is credited. No generic "second-line" costume.

designCues.cue: "Pretty": the Black Masking Indian ethic of a year of handwork, bead by bead, worn once in the street.
designCues.source: Big Chiefs such as Demond Melancon, and the Uptown and Downtown beadwork traditions.
designCues.use: A story of craft and refusal to bow down, told through one-of-one pieces a Big Chief makes on their own terms. Never print, scan or trace a suit or its patches.

productHooks: "Claiborne Oaks" Black history capsule: commission Tremé and Seventh Ward artists (BMike Odums, or artists in the Willie Birch lineage) to paint the lost live oaks back. Render them as wraparound side panels and a numbered print. Proceeds go to a Claiborne Corridor community group the artists choose.

"Throws" Carnival drop, from Twelfth Night (Jan 6) to Mardi Gras Day (Feb 9, 2027). It has two-sided Pelicans doubloon jock tags and tile-letter neighborhood tees. Float artists build a pop-up at Smoothie King Center.
Sign-painter wordmark line: a commissioned hand-lettered New Orleans alphabet with dot-border trims and glitter ink. Launch it at Art for Art's Sake or a Second Saturday on St. Claude.
"Streetcar" colorway: dark olive green with gold numerals and iron-lace laser-cut panels, for a fall shooting shirt, warm-up and lifestyle jacket.

One-of-one beaded patch by a Big Chief such as Demond Melancon, for a framed jersey or charity auction. Pay the full fee, give credit and leave the design to the chief. No printed beadwork on mass product.
Pre-cleared rapid-response tees with local makers like Fleurty Girl for big Zion or Trey Murphy III moments. That way the city's own tee vernacular becomes official product.
watchouts: Black Masking Indian suits, patches and roles are spiritual and ancestral, and each belongs to its maker. Never print, scan or trace them, and avoid headdress or "chief" iconography. Keep them separate from Native American imagery generally. Work only through named Big Chiefs and Big Queens, paid and credited.

Lead with something other than the fleur-de-lis. It reads as the Saints, and the 1724 Code Noir used it to brand enslaved people. After the 2010 "Who Dat" fight, any attempt to claim a local phrase or symbol will backfire.

Murals at Studio BE and on the Claiborne columns, krewe names and emblems (Rex, Zulu coconuts, Muses shoes), Jazz Fest marks and posters, Dr. Bob's "Be Nice or Leave" and Simon's signature style are all owned. License or commission them. Never lift them.
Don't decorate with Katrina. FEMA search "X-codes," water lines and flood imagery are trauma markers, and Lower Ninth Ward or Seventh Ward stories need local co-authors.

Bywater and St. Claude are gentrification flashpoints, and second lines are community property. Hire clubs, brass bands and Black New Orleans artists from the Seventh Ward, Ninth Ward and Central City. Don't stage a second line for marketing.
