food.headline: In New Orleans, the menu tells you what month it is
food.summary: New Orleans keeps time by what's in season: king cake from Twelfth Night to Mardi Gras, crawfish through Lent and Jazz Fest, sno-balls all summer, gumbo when the weather turns. Black Creole kitchens like Dooky Chase's and Willie Mae's anchor that calendar. After a 26-56 season under first-year coach Jamahl Mosley, city pride will sell more than the roster, and food is the sharpest clock for it.

insights.title: Carnival is the Pelicans' food season
insights.detail: King cake season runs from Twelfth Night (Jan 6) to Mardi Gras Day (Feb 9, 2027), right through the heart of the home schedule. Locals argue over cakes from Dong Phuong, Haydel's and Manny Randazzo. The Pelicans already own the food's best inside joke: the unnerving King Cake Baby mascot, which has haunted Carnival-season games since 2015.
insights.implication: Build the season's biggest city-specific drop around king cake, not generic beads. Release it on Jan 6, use the team-owned King Cake Baby, and pay a local bakery to make the co-branded box.

insights.title: Tremé's Black Creole kitchens are civic institutions
insights.detail: Leah Chase's Dooky Chase's fed Freedom Riders and civil rights organizers. It still serves gumbo z'herbes on Holy Thursday (Mar 25, 2027). A few blocks away, Willie Mae's Scotch House sets the city's fried-chicken benchmark. Both sit in the Tremé and Seventh Ward corridor that the I-10 Claiborne overpass cut through in the 1960s.
insights.implication: The deepest food story in this market is Black Creole and family-owned. Tell it only through paid partnerships with these families, and send proceeds back to the Claiborne corridor.

insights.title: The po-boy is a labor story on Central City bread
insights.detail: Locals trace the name to the 1929 streetcar strike, when ex-conductors Bennie and Clovis Martin fed striking "poor boys" for free. The loaf has come from Leidenheimer on Simon Bolivar Avenue in Central City since 1896. Ordering is coded: "dressed" means lettuce, tomato, pickle and mayo, and "debris" is the roast-beef gravy at Parkway.
insights.implication: A working-class origin story fits a team in a lean year. Use the butcher-paper wrap, the order ticket and the strike story for packaging and naming. Time it to the November Oak Street Po-Boy Festival.

insights.title: Vietnamese New Orleans makes Tết a home-market moment
insights.detail: Refugees who arrived after 1975 built Village de l'Est in New Orleans East around Mary Queen of Vietnam church. Its Tết festival falls near Lunar New Year (Feb 6, 2027), inside Carnival. Dong Phuong's loaves carry the city's banh mi, the "Vietnamese po-boys," and its king cake sells out every year. The West Bank (Gretna, Harvey) has its own pho-and-grocery corridor.
insights.implication: A Lunar New Year piece here is local, not borrowed from a coastal playbook. Co-design it with Vietnamese New Orleanian artists and Dong Phuong instead of using generic zodiac graphics.

insights.title: Second-line Sundays come with their own menu
insights.detail: From late summer to spring, yakamein ("Old Sober") vendors trail Social Aid and Pleasure Club parades through Tremé, the Seventh Ward and Central City. Ms. Linda Green, the Ya-Ka-Mein Lady, leads them in public. Front porches sell huckabucks, frozen Kool-Aid cups. The season lines up almost exactly with the NBA's October-to-June clock.
insights.implication: This is Black neighborhood culture, not set dressing. Work through Feed the Second Line and paid collabs with vendors and clubs. Never print club names or regalia without permission.

insights.title: The arena and the beer are already food brands
insights.detail: Fans watch games in an arena named for Smoothie King, founded in metro New Orleans in 1973. Owner Gayle Benson also owns Faubourg Brewing, which was renamed from Dixie Beer in 2020 over the name's Confederate associations. Pelicans game day is a quick downtown pre-game crowd. The big tailgate culture belongs to the Saints next door.
insights.implication: Clear the team's naming and beverage partners before any food collab. Keep the launch in the arena and along the Poydras corridor, not in a parking-lot tailgate.

insights.title: Crawfish and sno-balls bookend the stretch run
insights.detail: Crawfish boils peak from March to May, through Lenten fish fries and Jazz Fest (Crawfish Monica, cochon de lait po-boys). Sno-ball stands like Hansen's Sno-Bliz (since 1939) reopen in spring with nectar cream, a pink vanilla-almond flavor found almost nowhere else.
insights.implication: Give the late season and any play-in run its own palette: boiled-crawfish red and nectar pink. Don't reuse Carnival purple, green and gold.

places.name: Dooky Chase's Restaurant
places.why: Leah Chase's Creole dining room, where civil rights strategy was planned over gumbo, is the most respected food address in Black New Orleans.

places.name: Willie Mae's Scotch House
places.why: Its fried chicken won a James Beard America's Classic award in 2005. Volunteers rebuilt the place after Katrina, so it stands for neighborhood recovery.

places.name: Parkway Bakery & Tavern
places.why: Since 1911, this is where locals take visitors for the roast beef debris and fried shrimp po-boy. Its T-shirts are worn around town.

places.name: Leidenheimer Baking Company
places.why: It has baked the thin-crust French bread under most of the city's po-boys since 1896.

places.name: Dong Phuong Bakery
places.why: Its banh mi loaves and butter-and-cream-cheese king cake draw lines from every corner of the metro.

places.name: Hansen's Sno-Bliz
places.why: This family stand, open since 1939, is the reference point for shaved-ice sno-balls and house-made syrups like nectar cream.

places.name: Café Reconcile
places.why: It trains young New Orleanians for hospitality jobs over red beans and fried catfish on the Oretha Castle Haley corridor. A natural community partner.

places.name: Hong Kong Food Market
places.why: It anchors Vietnamese and pan-Asian grocery shopping on the West Bank, the other half of the city's Vietnamese food map.

places.name: Turkey and the Wolf
places.why: Mason Hereford's sandwich shop sells hand-scrawled, irreverent merch that young locals wear as a style signal.

places.name: Smoothie King Center
places.why: The home court is named for a smoothie chain founded in metro New Orleans. Its concession and beverage partners set the limits for any in-arena food collab.

people.name: Dooky Chase's (the Chase family)
people.role: Tremé restaurant family of Leah Chase (1923-2019), the 'Queen of Creole Cuisine'
people.why: Leah's grandson, chef Edgar "Dook" Chase IV, and the family keep up the Holy Thursday gumbo z'herbes and a dining room hung with African American art. Any Creole-pride product should start with their consent.

people.name: Ms. Linda Green, the Ya-Ka-Mein Lady
people.why: Her yakamein at second lines and Jazz Fest, plus national TV appearances, made "Old Sober" a citywide symbol of Black New Orleans street food.

people.name: Nina Compton
people.role: Saint Lucian-born chef of Compère Lapin; 2018 James Beard Best Chef: South
people.why: A finalist on Top Chef's New Orleans season, she became the city's leading Caribbean-Creole voice. She links New Orleans to the wider Black Atlantic table.

people.name: Serigne Mbaye
people.why: His tasting menu cooks the West African roots of Creole food (okra, rice, and gumbo's own name). A high-end voice for the diaspora story.

people.name: Mason Hereford
people.role: Chef-owner of Turkey and the Wolf and Molly's Rise and Shine
people.why: His thrift-store, hand-drawn design language and Bon Appétit's 2017 Best New Restaurant title turned a sandwich shop into a style reference for young locals.

people.name: Hubig's Pies
people.why: Its Savory Simon mascot became a cult T-shirt in the years the pies were gone, after the 2012 bakery fire and before they returned in 2022. That's proof that locals wear food brands as loyalty.

people.name: Krewe of Red Beans / Feed the Second Line
people.role: Lundi Gras bean-mosaic parade krewe and the culture-bearer nonprofit it started (founder Devin De Wulf)
people.why: The krewe turns a Monday dish into costume art. The nonprofit sends money to Black Masking Indians, second-line club members and musicians. Together they make a credible partner for red-beans product.

people.name: Poppy Tooker
people.role: Host of WWNO's 'Louisiana Eats!' and food historian
people.why: The city's best-known food explainer is the right person to check a food story before it goes on product.

moments.name: King cake season (Twelfth Night to Mardi Gras)
moments.why: It runs through prime home dates, king cakes fill every office, and the King Cake Baby comes out at Pelicans games.

moments.name: Tết at Mary Queen of Vietnam
moments.why: New Orleans East's biggest community gathering, full of food stalls, lands inside Carnival.

moments.name: Red Beans Parade (Krewe of Red Beans)
moments.why: Bean-mosaic costumes parade through the downtown neighborhoods and turn Monday's dish into wearable art.

moments.name: Holy Thursday gumbo z'herbes at Dooky Chase's
moments.why: Leah Chase's Lenten green gumbo is the year's most coveted lunch, and a late-season story moment.

moments.name: Crawfish season and Lenten Friday fish fries
moments.timing: Peaks March to May; Lenten Fridays Feb 12 - Mar 26, 2027
moments.why: Backyard boils and church fish fries are where fans gather during the stretch run.

moments.name: New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival
moments.timing: Last weekend of April and first weekend of May, Fair Grounds
moments.why: Its food booths (Crawfish Monica, cochon de lait po-boys, Ms. Linda's yakamein) are a city ritual. They collide with play-in and playoff dates.

moments.name: Treme Creole Gumbo Festival
moments.why: This free festival pairs gumbo with brass bands in Tremé during the first month of the season.

moments.name: Oak Street Po-Boy Festival
moments.why: A street festival for the city's sandwich, and a natural launch for po-boy product.

vocabulary.meaning: A po-boy with lettuce, tomato, pickles and mayo. "Shrimp, dressed" is a complete order.
The gravy-soaked roast-beef shreds from the pan, ordered on a po-boy (said DAY-bree).
A little something extra thrown in free (said LAN-yap). It covers any bonus.
Louis Armstrong's letter sign-off. It nods to the Monday red beans tradition that grew out of wash day.
A frozen Kool-Aid cup sold from a neighbor's front door. Also called a frozen cup or cold cup.
Yakamein: beef-noodle soup with egg and green onion, sold at second lines as a hangover cure.
The pink vanilla-almond sno-ball flavor, topped with condensed milk. It's a "sno-ball," never a snow cone.
Finding the plastic baby in your king cake slice. Whoever gets it buys the next cake.

designCues.cue: King cake sanding-sugar triad: purple #5B2C83, green #00843D and gold #F2B900 as glittering crystals over braided cinnamon-dough brown, not flat Carnival blocks.
designCues.source: The colored sugar on king cakes, in the Carnival colors Rex introduced in 1872.
designCues.use: A sugar-crystal speckle print or metallic-fleck knit for the January drop, so it reads as cake, not generic Mardi Gras.

designCues.cue: Nectar-cream pink #F5A3C7 with condensed-milk white #FFF8EC.
designCues.source: The pink nectar sno-ball at Hansen's and neighborhood stands.
designCues.use: A spring and summer colorway against Pelicans navy #0C2340 for shorts and sneaker accents that only locals will decode.

designCues.cue: Boiled-crawfish red #C2401F over a newspaper-covered boil table.
designCues.source: Backyard crawfish boils poured out onto newsprint from March to May.
designCues.use: Late-season and play-in warmups with a newsprint-grain texture. Never reproduce real newspaper mastheads.

designCues.cue: Powdered sugar dusted over chicory-coffee brown (base #3B2A20).
designCues.source: Beignets and café au lait, the French Market breakfast every local has eaten.
designCues.use: A soft sugar-dust gradient on dark fleece. No Café du Monde awning stripes or logos.

designCues.cue: Waxed white butcher-paper wrap with a hand-written "dressed" order ticket.
designCues.source: How po-boy shops wrap and ticket every sandwich, and the 1929 streetcar-strike "poor boy" origin.
designCues.use: Packaging, hangtags and shoebox tissue, with the strike origin printed inside the box.

designCues.cue: Hand-painted lettering from corner-store, po-boy and sno-ball stand signs: chunky brush capitals, drop shadows, hand-ruled menu boards.
designCues.source: Neighborhood corner stores and seasonal stands across the city.
designCues.use: Commission New Orleans sign painters to letter collection names and wordmarks. Credit them on the tag.

designCues.cue: The tiny plastic king cake baby as a hidden detail.
designCues.source: The baby baked into every king cake, and the Pelicans' own King Cake Baby mascot.
designCues.use: Hide it inside a collar, under a tongue or on a waistband tab. The mascot is team-owned IP, so it is clear to use.

designCues.cue: Red-bean mosaic: dried beans set like beadwork to form images.
designCues.source: Krewe of Red Beans costumes for the Lundi Gras Red Beans Parade.
designCues.use: Commission and pay krewe bean artists for an original graphic. Don't imitate Black Masking Indian beadwork.

productHooks: Twelfth Night Pack (Jan 6, 2027): a sanding-sugar knit warmup and tee in purple, green and gold, with a hidden King Cake Baby on the waistband. It ships in a king-cake-style box next to a paid, co-branded cake from a local bakery such as Dong Phuong.
"Dressed" Pelicans hoodie and tee, shipped in waxed butcher paper with an order-ticket hangtag and the 1929 "poor boy" story inside. Launch it at the November Oak Street Po-Boy Festival.

Nectar Cream colorway (pink #F5A3C7 on navy) for spring shorts and slides. If his Jordan Brand signature line is still active, add a Zion Williamson player-edition sneaker. Launch with a paid sno-ball stand collab.
Red Beans Monday tee for Monday home games, designed with Krewe of Red Beans artists. Proceeds go to Feed the Second Line.
Crawfish Season stretch-run pack: boiled-crawfish red warmups with a newsprint texture, timed to Lent and the Jazz Fest window.
Tết x Carnival capsule, co-designed with Vietnamese New Orleanian artists and launched at the Mary Queen of Vietnam festival weekend.
watchouts: Food brands are third-party IP. Café du Monde, Hubig's (Savory Simon), Zapp's (Utz), Barq's (Coca-Cola), Crystal (Baumer Foods), Camellia, Leidenheimer, Zatarain's (McCormick) and Kool-Aid (Kraft Heinz) all need licenses, so no lookalike trade dress. "Red Beans and Ricely Yours" ties to Louis Armstrong's legacy and needs clearance.

Second-line clubs, Black Masking Indian suits and the Holy Thursday table are Black community traditions. Don't lift club names, beadwork or vendors' identities. Credit and pay culture bearers directly or through Feed the Second Line.
Voodoo is a living religion. Skip voodoo-doll and "Voodoo" chip gimmicks, even though they're everywhere in the tourist food trade.
Smoothie King holds the arena naming rights and Gayle Benson owns Faubourg Brewing. Clear beverage categories with the team, and never revive Dixie Beer marks.

Tremé, the Seventh Ward and Central City face displacement, and the Claiborne overpass is still an open wound. Product that borrows their food without sending money back will be called out. Make no Katrina or Ida puns.

culture.headline: New Orleans pride outlasted the levees, and it lives ward by ward
culture.summary: New Orleans sees itself as America's original, the city that made jazz, Creole cooking, Carnival and bounce. It believes outsiders see a Bourbon Street party, a Katrina story or a crime headline. Pride is hyper-local: your ward, your high school, your club, your side of the river. The Pelicans are a young brand in a Saints-first town, so they earn loyalty by showing up in neighborhoods.

insights.title: A party or a problem, says everyone else
insights.detail: Locals believe the country knows New Orleans through Bourbon Street, 'N'awlins' and 'the Big Easy', or through Katrina, crime and the Jan 1, 2025 Bourbon Street truck attack. Their answer is authorship: Congo Square, jazz, Creole food, Carnival and bounce were made here, by them, in the northernmost port of the Caribbean.
insights.implication: Write product copy in local terms ('Where y'at', 'Yeah you right', ward numbers) and lead with the city as creator. Beads-and-booze, voodoo caricature and disaster imagery read as tourist or outsider gear.

insights.title: The levees, not the storm
insights.detail: Katrina hit on Aug 29, 2005. Locals stress that federal levee and floodwall failures put about 80% of the city under water. Families scattered to Houston, Atlanta and Baton Rouge, and neighborhoods like the Lower Ninth Ward emptied. The Saints' Superdome return on Sept 25, 2006 and the Super Bowl XLIV title in February 2010 became the civic resurrection. That's why the Saints still hold the city's emotional center.
insights.implication: Return and rebuild is the city's sacred text. Tell it only in local voices, with restraint, and keep Aug 29 for remembrance, not product. The Pelicans' honest angle is "still here," not borrowed resilience slogans.

insights.title: Basketball has left before
insights.detail: The ABA Buccaneers moved to Memphis in 1970. The Jazz (Pete Maravich's team) left for Salt Lake City in 1979 and kept the name. The Hornets played most of 2005-07 in Oklahoma City, which then landed the Thunder. The NBA owned the team from 2010 to 2012, then Tom Benson bought it and renamed it the Pelicans in 2013. Worry about permanence resurfaces in losing seasons like 2025-26's 26-56.
insights.implication: Fans reward permanence. Root the team in place (ward, high school, river, state bird). Honor the city's own hoops lineage, from Maravich to the Chris Paul Hornets and the All-Star Games of 2008, 2014 and 2017. A logo alone can't build that trust.

insights.title: Ward, school, side of the river
insights.detail: New Orleanians place each other by 'What school you went to?', meaning high school (St. Aug, Warren Easton, Edna Karr, McDonogh 35, Brother Martin, Jesuit, Newman), and by ward. Bounce records shout out wards by number (Third, Seventh, Ninth, Seventeenth). The West Bank (Algiers, Gretna, Marrero, Harvey), New Orleans East and 'Metry' each rep separately from the Eastbank core.
insights.implication: Build modular identity product: ward-numeral and high-school-coded pieces, made with local artists and the schools (licensed and paid). A fan then wears their exact New Orleans, not a generic city tee.

insights.title: Black and Creole institutions run the calendar
insights.detail: The city's defining traditions come from Black and Creole-of-color communities: Congo Square, Homer Plessy's 1892 test case (organized by Seventh Ward Creoles), Ruby Bridges at William Frantz in 1960 and the Claiborne Avenue oaks cut down for I-10. So do the living institutions of Black Masking Indians, Social Aid & Pleasure Clubs, Baby Dolls and Skull & Bone gangs. Each has its own rules, hierarchy and calendar (Mardi Gras Day, St. Joseph's Night, Super Sunday, Sunday second lines).
insights.implication: Co-create and pay. Commission chiefs, queens, club designers and Baby Doll groups, credit them by name, and time drops to their calendar. Never reproduce Indian suits, patches or chants on mass product.

insights.title: The pelican is a comeback story
insights.detail: The brown pelican is Louisiana's state bird. The 'pelican in her piety' (a mother feeding her chicks from her own breast) has been on the state flag and seal since the 19th century. DDT wiped out Louisiana's pelicans by the early 1960s. Birds reintroduced from Florida starting in 1968 recovered enough to leave the federal endangered list in 2009, a year before the BP spill put oiled pelicans on the news.
insights.implication: Give the team name a story locals can own: a self-sacrificing, back-from-zero bird that suits a rebuilding team. Put it on jock tags, liners and hangtags, not in the cartoon framing the 2013 rename was mocked for.

insights.title: Built for heat, costume and the Carnival-to-crawfish run
insights.detail: Summers are humid and stormy from May to September, and hurricane season runs June 1 to Nov 30. The mild months (October to May) carry the festivals: Twelfth Night, Carnival, Super Sunday, French Quarter Fest, Jazz Fest and crawfish season. Locals keep costume closets, mask for Carnival and Halloween, and treat Sunday second lines as best-dressed occasions.
insights.implication: The NBA season is New Orleans' outdoor season, so design for 60-80°F parade days: light layers, seersucker and mesh, rain shells, and pieces made to be customized or costumed. Concentrate drops between Jan 6 and the end of crawfish season, when the Pelicans have the city mostly to themselves.

places.name: Congo Square (Louis Armstrong Park)
places.why: Enslaved and free Africans gathered here on Sundays to drum, dance and trade. It's the root of the city's claim on American music.

places.name: Dooky Chase's Restaurant
places.why: Leah Chase's Creole dining room hosted civil rights strategy meetings and holds a major collection of Black art. Every Holy Thursday it serves gumbo z'herbes.

places.name: North Claiborne Avenue under the I-10 overpass
places.why: The Black business strip and oak-lined neutral ground that the interstate replaced in the late 1960s. It's still the gathering ground for Black Carnival on Mardi Gras Day.

places.name: A.L. Davis Park
places.why: The traditional starting point of Uptown Super Sunday, when Black Masking Indian gangs come out in their new suits.

places.name: William Frantz Elementary (now Akili Academy)
places.why: Six-year-old Ruby Bridges desegregated New Orleans public schools here on Nov 14, 1960. A statue of her stands at the school.

places.name: Plessy v. Ferguson marker, Press and Royal Streets
places.why: Marks where Homer Plessy was arrested in 1892, in a planned challenge by the Comité des Citoyens, a Creole civil rights group.

places.name: Hansen's Sno-Bliz
places.why: Family-run since 1939, and the benchmark for the sno-ball, the city's hot-weather ritual of finely shaved ice and syrups like nectar cream.

places.name: Dong Phuong Bakery
places.why: This Vietnamese bakery opened in 1982. Its king cakes and banh mi show how New Orleans East's Vietnamese community became part of Carnival.

places.name: Crescent City Connection
places.why: Twin cantilever spans link the Eastbank and West Bank across the river's crescent. This is the bridge in every skyline shot.

places.name: Caesars Superdome
places.why: The shelter of last resort during Katrina, site of the Saints' 2006 return, and home of the Bayou Classic and Essence Fest. Smoothie King Center is next door.

people.name: Allison "Tootie" Montana
people.role: Late Big Chief of the Yellow Pocahontas (Seventh Ward), called the 'Chief of Chiefs'
people.why: He shifted masking from street fights to a contest of beauty ('pretty'). He died in 2005 while telling the City Council about police treatment of Indians on St. Joseph's Night.

people.name: Cherice Harrison-Nelson
people.role: Big Queen of the Guardians of the Flame; founder of the Mardi Gras Indian Hall of Fame
people.why: A leading educator and gatekeeper for Black Masking culture. Partners like her should set the terms of any collaboration.

people.name: Leah Chase
people.role: Chef of Dooky Chase's (1923-2019), the 'Queen of Creole Cuisine'
people.why: She fed civil rights organizers, presidents and the Seventh Ward for seven decades. Her family still runs the restaurant.

people.name: Ruby Bridges
people.role: Civil rights icon; founder of the Ruby Bridges Foundation
people.why: The city's most recognized living civil rights figure, tied to the Upper Ninth Ward. Any school-integration story should go through her foundation.

people.name: Avery Johnson
people.role: St. Augustine High alum, 1999 NBA champion with the Spurs, former NBA and Alabama head coach
people.why: The 'Little General' embodies St. Aug pride and the city's high school basketball pipeline.

people.name: Chris Paul
people.role: Point guard of the New Orleans Hornets, 2005-2011
people.why: He carried the franchise through the Oklahoma City years and the 56-win 2007-08 season, which older fans remember as the team's peak.

people.name: Master P (Percy Miller)
people.role: No Limit Records founder from the Calliope projects (Third Ward)
people.why: A hoops-obsessed rap mogul (NBA preseason stints with Charlotte and Toronto). His 'Bout it' and 'Ya heard me' spread New Orleans slang nationally. UNO named him president of basketball operations in 2023.

people.name: Gayle Benson
people.role: Owner of the Pelicans and the Saints
people.why: One owner across both teams makes Saints-Pelicans cross-promotion possible during the Saints' offseason.

moments.name: Twelfth Night and king cake season
moments.why: Carnival opens with the Phunny Phorty Phellows streetcar ride and the Joan of Arc parade. King cake fills every office and locker room until Fat Tuesday.

moments.name: Mardi Gras Day
moments.why: Zulu and Rex roll. Black Masking Indians and Baby Dolls take the streets in Tremé and the Seventh Ward, Skull & Bone gangs wake the neighborhood at dawn, and St. Anne walks through the Marigny.

moments.name: St. Joseph's Night and Super Sunday
moments.timing: March 19 and the nearest Sunday (Uptown), with Downtown Super Sunday after
moments.why: The Black Masking Indians' other great outing, on the same day Sicilian families build St. Joseph's altars.

moments.name: New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival
moments.timing: Last weekend of April and first weekend of May, Fair Grounds Race Course
moments.why: The city's heritage showcase of music, food and crafts, with Mardi Gras Indian and second-line stages and parades.

moments.name: Essence Festival of Culture
moments.why: The country's largest Black culture festival, held at the Superdome and the convention center.

moments.name: Katrina anniversary
moments.why: A day of remembrance, marked with memorial second lines. Hurricane Ida also struck on Aug 29, 2021. It is not a commercial date.

moments.name: Second-line season
moments.why: Each Social Aid & Pleasure Club parades its neighborhood once a year in new colors behind a brass band, on almost exactly the NBA's calendar.

moments.name: Bayou Classic
moments.why: Southern vs. Grambling at the Superdome, with Friday's Battle of the Bands. It's the Gulf South's biggest HBCU homecoming.

vocabulary.meaning: The classic greeting ('How you doing?'). Answer 'Awright'. 'Yat' names the working-class accent that goes with it.
How's your whole family. It's a real question, not a throwaway.
Emphatic agreement, said almost as one word.
Grocery shopping, from the French 'faire son marché'.
The median. It comes from Canal Street, the strip between the Creole French Quarter and the American side, where parade crowds and streetcars sit.
Which high school. The answer places your neighborhood, class, race and faith at once.
A little something extra, given free. Local businesses still use the word and the practice.
An end-of-sentence tag meaning 'you understand?', carried nationally by Master P, Juvenile and Lil Wayne.

designCues.cue: City flag: red, white and blue horizontal bands with three gold fleurs-de-lis at the center.
designCues.source: Flag adopted for the 1918 bicentennial of the city's founding.
designCues.use: Lining print, jock tag or warm-up sleeve band. Draw the fleurs from the city flag, not in Saints-style black and gold.

designCues.cue: Pelican in her piety: a white pelican feeding three chicks from her breast, three red drops, over a ribbon reading 'Union, Justice, Confidence'. The 2006 flag redesign restored the drops.
designCues.source: Louisiana state flag and seal; the team's namesake bird.
designCues.use: Embroidered liner patch, hangtag or interior label that explains the name. Keep it reverent, since it's also Christian iconography, and check state seal usage rules.

designCues.cue: Ward numerals: heavy condensed ordinals ('7TH WARD', '9TH WARD', '17TH WARD') plus 'WESTBANK' and 'THE EAST', set like a bounce call-out.
designCues.source: Ward pride in bounce and rap shout-outs and in everyday 'where you stay' talk.
designCues.use: Chest and back numbers for a neighborhood pack, drawn by an artist from each ward. Skip demolished housing-project names unless former residents lead.

designCues.cue: Nectar cream pink (approx.), the pastel of New Orleans' signature sno-ball flavor.
designCues.source: Sno-ball stands like Hansen's Sno-Bliz; nectar is a vanilla-almond syrup rarely found outside the Gulf South.
designCues.use: Spring and summer accent against Pelicans Navy (#0C2340) on shooting shirts and lifestyle tees.

designCues.cue: Boil red (approx.), the orange-red of a fresh crawfish boil poured onto newspaper.
designCues.source: Crawfish season, peaking March to May, the backyard ritual that overlaps the Pelicans' stretch run.
designCues.use: A 'boil season' colorway with corn yellow and Pelicans Navy for March-April drops. Avoid cartoon crawfish.

designCues.cue: Seersucker: puckered cotton stripe that holds fabric off the skin in humidity.
designCues.source: Popularized by New Orleans clothier Joseph Haspel, who began making seersucker suits in 1909.
designCues.use: Navy-and-white seersucker panels or linings on warm-ups, shorts and lifestyle shirts. A collaboration with the Haspel brand would make it the true story.

designCues.cue: King cake: purple, green and gold sanding-sugar speckle plus the tiny plastic baby hidden inside.
designCues.source: King cake season (Jan 6 to Mardi Gras Day); whoever finds the baby buys the next cake.
designCues.use: A speckled tri-color knit or print as a Carnival texture that doesn't repeat the purple-and-neon 'Skelican' City Edition. Hide a small printed baby in a lining as an Easter egg.

designCues.cue: Brown pelican chestnut (approx.), the dark rust of the bird's breeding-season neck, paired with its white head and yellow crown.
designCues.source: Louisiana's state bird, off the endangered list since 2009.
designCues.use: A nature-true tonal colorway (chestnut, bone white, crown yellow) for lifestyle product that tells the comeback story.

productHooks: 'What School You Went To?' pack: Pelicans tees, hoodies and shorts co-branded with New Orleans high school programs (St. Aug, Easton, Karr, McDonogh 35, Brother Martin and others) under school licenses. Proceeds and gear go to their teams.

'Ward Call' neighborhood collection: ward-numeral jerseys and tees drawn by an artist from each ward, plus the West Bank and New Orleans East. Launch at ward-themed home nights between Twelfth Night and the All-Star break.
'Piety' story jacket: a navy warm-up with an embroidered pelican-in-her-piety liner and a 'Union, Justice, Confidence' hangtag that tells the brown pelican's comeback, for a rebuilding season.
'Boil Season' March-April drop: shooting shirts and shorts in boil red, nectar pink and seersucker panels, for the stretch run and any Play-In push (Apr 13-16, 2027). Built for 80°F days.

'Comité' Black History Month capsule: Plessy's 1892 stand, Ruby Bridges' 1960 walk and Dooky Chase's back room. Make it with the Plessy & Ferguson Foundation and the Ruby Bridges Foundation, which approve the work and share the proceeds.

Second-line co-sign: pay a Social Aid & Pleasure Club to design a limited Pelicans sash, umbrella and shirt in its own colors. Release it after the club's parade, so it never pre-empts the color reveal.
watchouts: Black Masking Indian suits, patches, songs and gang names are sacred. They represent a year of handwork and belong to their makers. Never print or imitate them, never use Native American headdress imagery, and use 'Black Masking Indians' or a gang's own name only with permission.

Katrina is grief, not a theme. Skip flood waterlines, search-and-rescue X-codes, blue tarps and Superdome-shelter imagery. Run nothing commercial on Aug 29, and don't frame the Jan 1 anniversary of the 2025 attack as a Bourbon Street party.

Clear licensing for the Saints' fleur-de-lis rendering, krewe names, emblems and throws such as Zulu coconuts, high school marks, and Norman Rockwell's Ruby Bridges painting. 'Who Dat' needs clearance too: the NFL's 2010 cease-and-desist push against local tee makers caused a public backlash.

Don't flatten the region. Cajun means Acadiana (Lafayette), not New Orleans Creole. Locals don't say 'N'awlins' or 'the Big Easy'. Louisiana Voodoo is a living religion, not a costume or skull graphic.
Use current place names. After the 2017 Confederate monument removals, Lee Circle became Harmony Circle and Jefferson Davis Parkway became Norman C. Francis Parkway.

underground.headline: New Orleans style is set on the parade route, not in a skate shop
underground.summary: The strongest scenes here are living street traditions: Social Aid & Pleasure Club second lines, bounce with its queer-led core, and the Black Masking Indians. They dress to be seen moving, so color-matched sneakers, custom suits and hand-painted detail beat logos. Start with neighborhoods, not a hype launch. Leave everything ceremonial alone, and pay and credit every local partner.

insights.title: The second line is a sneaker runway
insights.detail: Social Aid & Pleasure Clubs such as the Original Big 7, Black Men of Labor, Young Men Olympian Jr. and the Lady Buckjumpers parade most Sundays from fall to spring. They wear custom suits, sashes, hats and fans, with shoes color-matched to each club's season outfit. Fresh Air Force 1s, Jordans and dress-casual sneakers are part of the look.
insights.implication: Offer clean, tonal sneaker colorways that can match a club's colors. Approach clubs about a commissioned, credited colorway, and keep the swoosh off their regalia.

insights.title: Bounce is the city's own sound, built by queer artists
insights.detail: Bounce grew out of Magnolia and Calliope-era housing-project parties. Big Freedia, Katey Red, Sissy Nobby and DJ Jubilee carried it forward. Outsiders miss its dance language (the shake, the buck) and its queer and trans center.
insights.implication: Build events with bounce DJs and dancers on the stipend roster, and treat the queer artists as lead voices. Design for movement: stretch, breathable, loose layers that survive a sweaty dance floor.

insights.title: Black Masking Indian craft is sacred, not a mood board
insights.detail: Black Masking Indian tribes sew new suits every year from beads, feathers and rhinestones. Super Sunday and St. Joseph's night are the main gatherings. The Backstreet Cultural Museum in Tremé is the community-run archive of the tradition.
insights.implication: Keep suit imagery, patches and tribe iconography off product. If Nike engages at all, go through the Backstreet Museum and tribal members, on their terms, with payment and veto power.

insights.title: The tee economy runs on phrases, not logos
insights.detail: Local brands like Dirty Coast turned neighborhood talk and in-jokes into the city's best-selling tees, and locals wear them over team gear. The more specific the reference, the stronger the sign of belonging.
insights.implication: Set ward, neighborhood and phrase typography on tees that sit alongside the City Edition. Consider partnering with a local brand rather than using an outside agency voice.

insights.title: St. Claude and the Bywater hold the DIY layer
insights.detail: Zeitgeist Multi-Disciplinary Arts Center, the AllWays Lounge and the Hi-Ho Lounge anchor the experimental, zine, drag and punk crowd along St. Claude Avenue and in the Marigny. Vintage and thrift buyers work Magazine Street and the Bywater, mixing old Saints, Hornets and Pelicans jerseys with local tees.
insights.implication: Source heritage Hornets teal-and-purple and early Pelicans looks for a vintage-inspired capsule. Seed it through these venues and local thrift buyers, not mall retail.

insights.title: Zion fandom is loyal but frustrated
insights.detail: A second straight sub-30-win season (26-56), a quiet offseason and new coach Jamahl Mosley leave fans loyal to the city and club but less sold on the roster. Trey Murphy III, Derik Queen and Jeremiah Fears are the younger names the street-level crowd can adopt.
insights.implication: Lead with city identity and rising players, not a title story. Keep the team tie light and let neighborhoods carry the story.

Neighborhood-court refurbishment in Tremé or the Seventh Ward with local muralists, to support the underground, not extract from it.

Pelican team marks, Hornets heritage marks, Saints and "Who Dat" references each need separate licensing. Confirm before using.
Skip tourist-register imagery (Bourbon Street, fleur-de-lis in isolation, voodoo). The local underground reads it as a tell.

hoops.headline: In New Orleans, the high school gym outranks the NBA arena
hoops.summary: Basketball in New Orleans is school pride first. Edna Karr, St. Augustine, Warren Easton and the rest command more block-level loyalty than any pro team. The Pelicans come off a 26-56 season, their second straight under 30 wins, so local identity is the way in, not winning. Go through gyms, school programs and Black-led cultural institutions, with credit and payment.

insights.title: School colors outrank the NBA team
insights.detail: St. Augustine (Purple Knights), Edna Karr, Warren Easton, McDonogh 35, Landry-Walker and John Curtis carry multi-generational loyalty. A Friday-night or district-rivalry game is a bigger local event than a midweek Pelicans game in a losing season.
insights.implication: Build school and neighborhood collections and team-sale programs, not just Pelicans merch. A purple-and-gold or maroon school-pride capsule reads as local in a way an NBA logo doesn't.

insights.title: A rebuilding team and tired fans
insights.detail: The Pelicans have had two straight sub-30-win seasons, a coaching change (Willie Green out, Jamahl Mosley in), no 2026 first-round pick and a quiet summer under Joe Dumars. Fans are fatigued, though Zion Williamson and Trey Murphy III still draw attention.
insights.implication: Lead with the city and its hoopers, not the standings. Product that celebrates New Orleans holds its value when the team isn't winning.

insights.title: Heat and humidity set the on-court look
insights.detail: Summer and early-fall runs happen in extreme humidity, in open-air or poorly cooled neighborhood gyms. Hoopers wear breathable mesh, sleeveless or short-sleeve tops, and layered tees for the walk to the court.
insights.implication: Prioritize ultra-light mesh and moisture-wicking Dri-FIT pieces, plus shorter-sleeve shooting shirts. Cold-weather hoops product matters less here than in Portland.

insights.title: Second lines and Mardi Gras set the look
insights.detail: Neighborhood social aid and pleasure clubs, brass bands and Mardi Gras parades set a color and movement vocabulary of purple, green, gold, sequins and fringe that locals recognize instantly.
insights.implication: Borrow the palette and rhythm of celebration for City Edition and lifestyle pieces. Keep sacred Black Masking Indian suiting imagery off product unless a Black Masking Indian partner leads and is paid.

insights.title: Little pro basketball beyond the Pelicans
insights.detail: The market has no WNBA team. The Pelicans' G League affiliate, the Birmingham Squadron, plays in Alabama, so there's no in-city pro alternative. Tulane, UNO and the HBCUs fill the college gap.
insights.implication: The grassroots and school scene is the real on-ramp. Sponsor clinics, courts and camps, and don't expect a pro-team halo from a second franchise.

insights.title: Louisiana legends belong to the whole state
insights.detail: Louisiana's hoops pride leans on Pete Maravich and Shaq at LSU, and on Louisiana-born greats Bill Russell and Willis Reed. New Orleans locals fold them into a Gulf South identity.
insights.implication: Legacy stories and throwback-inspired pieces can borrow a Gulf South heritage frame. Check rights and estate permissions for any product that names or pictures a player.

fanbase.headline: Pelicans fans are weary of waiting on Zion, not angry
fanbase.summary: New Orleans is a Saints, LSU and Mardi Gras town first. The Pelicans hold a loyal, modest slice of it, strongest among diehards who stayed through the Hornets-to-Pelicans change. Two straight sub-30-win seasons (26-56 last year) have left the mood weary, not angry. Fans wear the city alongside the team: fleur-de-lis, purple-green-gold, local brands next to navy and gold. The best City Editions did the same.

insights.title: Saints first, Pels second
insights.detail: Football, LSU and Carnival dominate the calendar and the closet. Pelicans gear competes with black-and-gold Saints and purple-and-gold LSU apparel for the same wardrobe slot. Pelicans passion is real but concentrated, and it peaks when the team tells a New Orleans story instead of a generic NBA one.
insights.implication: Lead Pelicans product with city iconography (fleur-de-lis, Carnival, second line), not team marks alone. Don't copy Saints black and gold.

insights.title: Fatigue, not fury
insights.detail: Last season ended 26-56, the second straight sub-30-win year, with no playoffs. Now fans face a coach change from Willie Green to Jamahl Mosley, no 2026 first-round pick (traded to Atlanta in the Derik Queen deal) and a quiet summer.
insights.implication: Keep early-season product and campaigns about the city and the young core, not championship promises. Trey Murphy III, Queen and Fears are safer faces than anything built on Zion's availability.

insights.title: Zion is the brand, Murphy is the trust
insights.detail: Zion Williamson draws national attention and the biggest jersey and sneaker interest. Years of injuries have made fans wary of hanging their identity on him. Trey Murphy III averaged 21.5 ppg and survived June trade rumors. Locals admire him as a homegrown-feeling scorer.
insights.implication: Balance Zion signature product with Murphy and young-core pieces, so one availability story doesn't govern the line. Zion is already a Jordan Brand athlete, so coordinate any Jordan crossover.

insights.title: Hornets memory runs deep
insights.detail: Older fans remember the 2002-2013 Hornets: Chris Paul, David West, Tyson Chandler, Byron Scott. They remember the 2005-07 Oklahoma City exile after Katrina too. Teal and purple Hornets throwbacks still circulate, and the Pelicans name only arrived in 2013.
insights.implication: A teal and purple heritage nod could land with these fans. The Hornets name and marks belong to Charlotte, so clear the licensing first.

insights.title: City Edition is the fan favorite
insights.detail: Per the current facts, the 2025-26 City Edition revived the fan-favorite 2023-24 design. That signals fans reward local stories and punish the generic. The 2023-24 "NOLA Nights" edition (purple and neon green, a skeletal "Skelican") shows they prefer a nocturnal, local look to plain team color.
insights.implication: Make the City Edition the market's anchor drop. Pair it with a lifestyle capsule built on Carnival color blocking, made with local collaborators.

insights.title: Don't lift Black Masking Indian imagery
insights.detail: Black Masking Indian suits are sacred community traditions, and the maskers spend a full year making them. The same goes for the Tremé and Seventh Ward second-line brass-band culture. Fans love and display the culture, but the community guards it.
insights.implication: Credit and pay Black New Orleans partners for any reference. Never reproduce the suits as a pattern. Safer cues are the bold, unaffiliated looks of Carnival parades, social aid and pleasure club umbrella and sash colors, and brass-band typography.

rhythm.headline: In New Orleans, Carnival eats February and the Pelicans fit in around it
rhythm.summary: The Pelicans fan year runs on low expectations and high loyalty: 26-56 last season, a new coach and no 2026 first-round pick. Interest peaks from late October through December. Then Carnival takes January and February, and Jazz Fest, crawfish and hurricane season take the rest. Fans buy culture first and team second, so the best retail moments meet Mardi Gras, second lines or Essence weekend.

insights.title: Carnival is the real February
insights.detail: Carnival season starts January 6, and Mardi Gras Day is February 9, 2027. The trade deadline (Feb 11) and All-Star weekend (Feb 19-21) land right on the post-Carnival hangover. Parade routes, school closures and the krewe calendar rule. Pelicans games compete with Endymion, Bacchus and Zulu weekends.
insights.implication: Don't launch a Pelicans hero drop in the two weeks before Mardi Gras. Instead, run Carnival-adjacent product (purple, green and gold throwback energy, throw-style graphics) as a January pre-sale that can bridge to the team.

insights.title: Saints Sundays and LSU Saturdays own the fall
insights.detail: Saints games and LSU football in Baton Rouge fill September through early January. The Pelicans opener (the league tips off Oct 20; their own date is still to confirm) and the November Cup nights compete with football. Casual fans tune in more once the Saints season ends in January.
insights.implication: Time drops to Friday Cup nights and weekday evenings, and don't fight Sunday. Co-brand around Gulf South pride, not Saints marks. The Saints and Pelicans share an owner, so check licensing and the relationship before any joint story.

insights.title: Cup group play is the early hook
insights.detail: The Pelicans are in NBA Cup West Group B with OKC, Minnesota, the Clippers and Memphis, opening Oct 30 at the Clippers. Cup games land on Fridays. Memphis is the nearest regional rivalry on the schedule.
insights.implication: Use Cup nights for a limited Cup-colorway or Friday-night capsule. A Memphis game is the natural Gulf South and Mississippi River story for a regional graphic.

insights.title: Hope follows players, not results
insights.detail: Two straight sub-30-win seasons have fans attaching to individuals: Zion Williamson, Trey Murphy III (who survived June trade rumors), and second-year players Derik Queen and Jeremiah Fears. A new coach adds a fresh-start story in October.
insights.implication: Lead with player product: Murphy and Zion signature or player-edition apparel, and youth sizing for Queen and Fears. Treat playoff gear as an upside scenario only.

insights.title: Spring belongs to the city
insights.detail: If the team misses the playoffs again, April and May belong to Jazz Fest (late April to early May), crawfish boils and festival season, and the Pelicans nearly vanish. The draft lottery and a possible high pick bring back some interest.
insights.implication: Treat April and May as a non-basketball window. Sell lightweight festival-ready apparel, and show up with Nike Basketball on neighborhood courts and in brass-band culture, not with Pelicans performance gear.

insights.title: Summer is hot and full of visitors
insights.detail: June to September means heat, afternoon storms and hurricane season. Essence Festival, around July 4, brings a huge influx of Black visitors and national culture to the Superdome and Smoothie King Center area. Southern Decadence at Labor Day draws another tourist wave.
insights.implication: Essence weekend is the best summer moment for retail and a collaboration with Black-owned creators. Pelicans product sold to visitors has to read as New Orleans, not generic NBA.

uniform.headline: Fans want the city's real second-line color on the jersey, not the tourist version
uniform.summary: The Pelicans launched in 2013 in navy, gold and red, and the Hornets' teal and purple stayed in Charlotte. With no classic era to mine, fans find their identity in New Orleans-made merch. The 2023-24 "NOLA Nights" City Edition was loved enough to return in 2025-26. The opening is local stories, built with the people who own those traditions.

insights.title: Young identity, no classic vault
insights.detail: The Pelicans brand dates to 2013, and the 2002-13 Hornets history sits with Charlotte. There is no multi-decade throwback vault to mine. Fans' emotional anchors are Anthony Davis, Chris Paul-era Hornets memories and Zion.
insights.implication: Classic Edition is a weak lever here. Put design energy into City Edition and lifestyle product built from the city, not the franchise archive.

insights.title: A returning City Edition shows what fans want
insights.detail: The 2025-26 City Edition reissued the 2023-24 design, which fans had singled out as a favorite. A team repeating a City Edition is a sign of unusually strong demand for one look.
insights.implication: Study what made the 2023-24 design land before briefing a 2026-27 concept, and don't swap it for something more generic. Verify the 2026-27 City Edition status first.

insights.title: Carnival colors are expected, and flat
insights.detail: Purple, green and gold is the city's default shorthand. The 2023-24 "Skelican" edition used purple and neon green, but as a night-life look. Locals take Carnival color for granted, so they respond more to specifics: krewe culture, the Zulu and Rex traditions, and the neighborhood second-line clubs.
insights.implication: Skip the generic three-color stripe. Use named, credited local references, with purple, green and gold used with restraint against navy.

insights.title: Real merch lives outside the team shop
insights.detail: Local screen-printed shirts, Who Dat-style vernacular, Saints and Pelicans crossovers and neighborhood-pride tees (Seventh Ward, Ninth Ward, Westbank, Uptown) outsell generic team gear. Fans trade on area codes, wards and slang.
insights.implication: Work with local New Orleans printers and designers. Build neighborhood-first graphics that the team's own shop doesn't.

insights.title: The biggest untouched design language
insights.detail: Black Masking Indian suits, hand-sewn beadwork and feather work, and brass-band second-line parades from the Tremé and Seventh Ward are the city's most distinctive visual tradition. They are sacred and living, not decoration.
insights.implication: Treat it as a partnership, and credit and pay the tribes' and artists' communities. Borrow the logic (color layering, patchwork, hand-stitched texture), not the suit imagery.

insights.title: Zion and Murphy lead a rebuilding team
insights.detail: After two sub-30-win seasons, a 26-56 record and a coaching change to Jamahl Mosley, fan sentiment is cautious. Zion Williamson is still the marquee jersey. Trey Murphy III, Derik Queen and Jeremiah Fears are the younger faces.
insights.implication: Back player product (Zion, Murphy) and city pride, not team-performance stories. Keep launch volume measured.

retail-landscape.headline: New Orleans sets its taste on Magazine Street and moves its volume in the suburbs
retail-landscape.summary: Basketball is a small business here next to football and Mardi Gras. The Saints and local city-pride brands own the Gulf South gear wallet, and the Pelicans sit below them. Taste lives in a few uptown and Bywater shops and at pop-ups. Volume lives in Metairie, Gretna and Kenner, and online. The job is to earn city-pride credibility, not to add square footage.

insights.title: City pride outsells the Pelicans
insights.detail: Locals wear fleur-de-lis, 'Who Dat' and NOLA-pride tees from brands like Dirty Coast and Fleurty Girl every day. Pelicans gear fights for the same shirt-drawer slot, and fans often wear city-first, not team-first.
insights.implication: Put New Orleans iconography first and the team mark second on Pelicans and City Edition product. It should pass as city pride, not team merch.

insights.title: Taste on Magazine Street, volume in Jefferson Parish
insights.detail: Uptown Magazine Street holds the independent boutiques and vintage. The Lakeside, Riverwalk and West Bank (Oakwood) malls hold the athletic chains and department stores where families buy sneakers and jerseys.
insights.implication: Seed limited drops and collabs in tastemaker doors and local pop-ups. Then send mainstream colorways to Foot Locker, Dick's and Dillard's in the suburbs.

insights.title: Sneaker culture is community-run
insights.detail: New Orleans has fewer destination sneaker boutiques than Atlanta or Houston. The culture runs through school and AAU hoops, park courts, resale meetups and Black-owned apparel brands. Much of it sells through social media and pop-ups.
insights.implication: Fund local creators and pop-up hosts instead of a single flagship. Treat the Instagram-driven local sellers as the retail scene.

insights.title: The arena store is a game-night door
insights.detail: The Pelicans Team Store at Smoothie King Center and the arena's pop-up kiosks catch event-night buyers. The season-ticket base is modest after two sub-30-win seasons, and Jamahl Mosley is the new coach. Fanatics and the team's online store carry the rest of the team-gear volume.
insights.implication: Use the arena store for City Edition launches, Zion and Trey Murphy III player-tee drops and Cup-night giveaways. Keep deep inventory online.

insights.title: Tourists skew the Quarter and Canal Street
insights.detail: Canal Place, Riverwalk and the Quarter's souvenir shops see huge traffic. It is visitor spend on Saints, Mardi Gras and generic NOLA gear, not local basketball demand.
insights.implication: Treat tourist districts as places for brand visibility and Mardi Gras-season merchandising. Don't read them as a gauge of local Pelicans demand.

insights.title: Black Masking Indian imagery is off limits without a deal
insights.detail: Suits, feathers and beadwork belong to specific Black neighborhood tribes and the social aid and pleasure clubs. The community guards how they are used, and commercial lifting without credit has drawn criticism.
insights.implication: Work only through paid collaboration with named artists and clubs. Keep product abstracted from ceremonial imagery.

retail-behavior.headline: In New Orleans, Carnival and festivals get the money before the Pelicans do
retail-behavior.summary: This is a high-tourism, moderate-income market. People dress for parades, second lines, tailgates and festivals, and heat and humidity rule most of the year. Locals watch the price tag, while visitors pay more for anything city-specific. Team gear rides on Zion Williamson, Trey Murphy III and the City Edition, not on winning.

insights.title: Carnival is the first-quarter peak
insights.detail: Carnival runs from Twelfth Night (Jan 6) to Mardi Gras Day, which falls on Feb 9 in 2027. In the weeks before, locals buy purple, green and gold gear, throw-related items and parade-day outfits. The Pelicans' home calendar competes with parade routes, and many fans plan around krewe schedules.
insights.implication: Have a Carnival-adjacent capsule ready by mid-January, not February. Keep it about the city's wardrobe (hoodies, tees, caps), not literal throws or krewe marks.

insights.title: Light layers, with a short winter
insights.detail: Summers are hot and humid, hurricane season runs June to November, and rain is frequent year-round. Genuine cold lasts a few weeks between December and February. Fans buy shorts and breathable tees far longer than in northern markets, and add a hoodie or light jacket for cold snaps and over-air-conditioned arenas.
insights.implication: Weight assortments toward lightweight tees, shorts, quarter-zips and water-resistant shells. Keep outerwear thin, packable and rain-ready, not heavy puffer.

insights.title: Festivals outrank the NBA calendar for spend
insights.detail: Four events pull big shopper crowds that overlap with the NBA offseason or the start of fall. Essence Festival of Culture runs over July 4 weekend. Jazz Fest runs late April into early May. The Bayou Classic (Grambling vs Southern in the Superdome) takes Thanksgiving weekend, and Southern Decadence takes Labor Day weekend. Essence brings a national Black audience with real spending power.
insights.implication: Plan pop-ups and city-product drops around Essence and the Bayou Classic. They reach locals and out-of-town buyers when the Pelicans aren't playing. Partner with HBCU and Black-owned local voices.

insights.title: Sunday second lines drive local social commerce
insights.detail: Social aid and pleasure clubs parade most Sundays from roughly September to May in custom-dyed matching outfits. The outfits, suits, fans and sneakers are commissioned and photographed heavily on Instagram. Mardi Gras Indian culture keeps a parallel, craft-based season, with Super Sunday in March and St. Joseph's night around March 19.
insights.implication: Treat second-line fashion as a custom, color-matched, sneaker-forward market. Offer coordinated team colorways and customization, and hire the clubs as paid collaborators instead of borrowing their imagery.

insights.title: Price-sensitive locals, bigger-spending visitors
insights.detail: Orleans Parish has a large lower-income population and a hospitality workforce paid in tips. Cash flow follows tourist seasons, tax-refund season and Carnival work. Visitors buy a premium souvenir piece, and often a jersey, on a trip.
insights.implication: Tier the range. Offer accessible swingman, kids and tees for local households, and a premium city-keepsake tier and authentic pieces for visitors and out-of-state Pelicans fans.

insights.title: The Pelicans compete with Saints, LSU and Tulane
insights.detail: Football (Saints, LSU in Baton Rouge, Tulane) and the Sugar Bowl on New Year's Day set the fall and winter fan calendar. Pelicans gear is often the second or third team purchase. Sentiment is cool: the team went 26-56, its second straight sub-30-win season, and had a quiet offseason with no 2026 first-round pick.
insights.implication: Lead with Zion, Trey Murphy III, Derik Queen, Jeremiah Fears and the City Edition, not the standings. Use Cup nights and the new-coach story for early-season hooks.

extra.priceProfile: Orleans Parish is lower-income with a high poverty rate, alongside an affluent Uptown and Garden District. Household cash flow is tied to tips and seasonal hospitality work. Locals respond to accessible prices, bundles and kids' value tiers. Visitors will pay for a premium or limited city-specific piece. Louisiana's combined state and Orleans local sales tax is roughly 10 percent as of 2025, and there is no standing back-to-school tax holiday, so read price tags as all-in at checkout.
extra.jerseyBehavior: Local fans lean toward swingman jerseys and tees at lower prices, and kids' jerseys are the big gift item. Committed fans and visitors buy most of the authentic jerseys. Zion Williamson is the leading name, with Trey Murphy III rising, and the City Edition is the big limited moment. Knockoffs and unlicensed festival-vendor shirts are part of the local streetwear economy and set the price anchor for official product.

factcheck.summary: The dossiers are largely accurate on the Pelicans' 2026-27 facts, the Cup schedule and the Carnival dates. A live check found one big error: the City Edition brought back in 2025-26 is the purple-and-neon-green "NOLA Nights" Skelican edition, not a Mardi Gras one. Five dossiers are fixed, and the brief's "Carnival palette is spent" rationale is flagged for the editor. The rest are smaller fixes and claims that still need a live check.

issues.problem: The brief treats Corner Tile as if it could reach the court soon. But the 2026-27 City Edition is already designed, approved and in production, and the brief never calls Corner Tile a 2027-28 concept. The calendar doesn't set the NBA approval window for the next set, and the Association set is already white-based.
issues.fix: Label Corner Tile as the 2027-28 City Edition pitch, with a back-planned approval timeline. For 2026-27, put the tile, iron-lace and ward language on lifestyle product that rides the existing City Edition. Pull Glazed White as the base, or define it against the Association white, since NBA rules require the two sets to contrast.

issues.problem: Ward Call launches at a "home opener" whose date is unverified. The Oct 20 opening-night slate doesn't include New Orleans, and the first known Pelicans game is Oct 30 at the Clippers. The pack also needs one paid artist per ward, many school licenses, high-school sign-offs and a Big Freedia booking within about 3 weeks.
issues.fix: Phase it. Launch with 2 or 3 wards and a handful of schools at the first confirmed home game. Roll out the full 17 wards and the school co-brands from December to February. Hold the Freedia set until her footwear and apparel status is cleared, and lead with a bounce lineup of named queer pioneers (Katey Red, Sissy Nobby).

issues.problem: Licensed co-brands with St. Aug, Edna Karr, Warren Easton and McDonogh 35 involve minors, school marks and athletic departments that may be tied to other brands. LHSAA, Orleans Parish and charter-network rules apply too. The brief calls this licensing but names no process.
issues.fix: Start with one willing program or alumni association. Route everything through the school's licensing and athletic office, and make the giveback (gear, gym or team funds) the headline. Treat the school line as a 2027 phase-two item, not an October launch item.

issues.problem: The Bayou Classic band collaboration is built around St. Augustine's Marching 100, a New Orleans high school band. But the Battle of the Bands is between Southern and Grambling. The drop also lands on Nov 27, a Cup Friday, with the Superdome area full of rival-brand HBCU tailgates.
issues.fix: Either center the Bayou Classic piece on HBCU-coded product, using the two universities' own licensing and band programs (and Xavier and Dillard locally). Or keep the St. Aug collaboration as a separate local brass story outside Classic weekend. Check the Pelicans' Nov 27 schedule before planning a pop-up.

issues.problem: One headline artist is carrying the whole bounce story. Bounce credit belongs to a group (Katey Red, Sissy Nobby, DJ Jubilee and others), so a single paid booking risks reading as star-casting. Her footwear and apparel obligations are also unknown.
issues.fix: Pay a rotating roster of bounce artists and DJs for the ward call-and-response. Put the credit on the product and in the arena, and offer the commission to bounce pioneers before the headliner.

issues.target: partners[Dirty Coast, Fleurty Girl] rapid-response tees
issues.problem: The plan has local brands make quick player tees. But player names and numbers fall under NBA and NBPA group licensing, which a local brand can't sublicense, and the brief itself notes the "Who Dat" history. Without those approvals, a pre-cleared program isn't feasible on a turnaround of days.
issues.fix: Make the rapid-response tees city-only, with no player likenesses. Or get Pelicans and NBPA clearance up front for a fixed list of designs and a fixed turn time. Keep the local brands as co-designers of the voice, and pay them as such.

issues.problem: The Twelfth Night Pack leans on purple, green and gold, yet the brief says the Carnival palette is spent and the fan-favorite City Edition already owns it. The King Cake Baby hunt and co-branded cake are fun but thin as a design idea. The food co-brand also has shipping, shelf-life and food-safety limits.
issues.fix: Keep the sanding-sugar texture and the Baby, but cut the palette to a navy ground with a small fleck. Run the cake as an in-arena giveaway, not a bundled retail item. Confirm Pelicans ownership of the King Cake Baby for apparel before building around it.

issues.problem: A Tết x Carnival tee ties a church-centered family holiday to Carnival, with a short window before Mardi Gras Day. Pairing a community's New Year with a Carnival theme risks making it a novelty. The brief also names the Mary Queen of Vietnam gathering in a drop plan.
issues.fix: Move it off the product calendar. Instead, fund or host a community moment: pay Vietnamese New Orleanian artists to design a Pelicans game-night element, or name Dong Phuong as a food partner. Ask the community whether it wants a product at all.

issues.problem: The plan assumes "Cup Friday home nights", a Memphis rivalry graphic and a Cup-colorway capsule. But only the Oct 30 Cup opener (at the Clippers) is known, and the home dates are unconfirmed. There's also no Cup-specific uniform, only the standard sets, so the brief can't promise a Cup colorway.
issues.fix: Tie Cup events to confirmed home dates only, and use a generic Friday-night-in-New-Orleans graphic that works against any Cup opponent. Drop the "Cup colorway" language. Keep the Memphis graphic only if the home date is confirmed.

issues.target: calendar (Oak Street Po-Boy Festival, Red Beans Monday tee)
issues.problem: A hoodie wrapped in butcher paper and a Monday red-beans tee are novelty food references with no clear fan, price or reason to buy. The November hoodie is for a festival that is only a day of walking. Beside the stronger craft ideas, they read like tourist-guide gags.
issues.fix: Fold them into one community gesture: pay Feed the Second Line and the Krewe of Red Beans to design a Monday home-night element. Cut the Po-Boy Festival item.

issues.problem: The club commission is the best idea in the brief. But the plan has Nike underwriting parade permits and police fees, and pushes a release "the week after the parade" as a limited sneaker. Club colors stay secret until parade day. A release that depends on a club's schedule, can't be previewed and needs its sign-off clashes with Nike's lead times. It could also read as buying the culture.
issues.fix: Make the first season a no-product pilot. Pay the club and band, fund the fees through a culture-bearer intermediary, and let the club decide whether and when product exists. Plan a numbered, small-run, club-owned release only if the club asks for one.

issues.problem: The brief gives the museum "veto rights" as an introducer and advisor. But the museum is a small community institution, not a gatekeeper for every club or tribe. The clubs and tribes must consent for themselves.
issues.fix: Treat the museum as one paid advisor and ask it who else should be at the table. Get written consent from each club and band directly. Keep the Black Masking Indian line as "no product, no reference", and don't use Super Sunday or St. Joseph's Night in any plan.

issues.problem: The Claiborne Oaks story turns a documented loss to a Black neighborhood, the overpass that removed the oaks, into a product theme. It's credible only if the artists lead. Putting it on an NBA uniform as an alternate puts a community wound under a swoosh.
issues.fix: Keep it as an artist-owned capsule, with the artists choosing the beneficiary and the credit. Take it off the uniform alternates list. Brief it to Studio BE only as an invitation, with room to decline.

issues.target: topInsights and collection (fleur-de-lis and Code Noir)
issues.problem: The avoid list states the Code Noir fleur-de-lis point as settled fact. The mark's historical use in branding is real, but how the story is told is contested. The Pelicans' own mark also uses the fleur-de-lis, so the brief's stance conflicts with the team's identity.
issues.fix: Say plainly that the fleur-de-lis is avoided mainly because it reads as Saints and as tourist shorthand. Give the history as a secondary reason, and note that the Pelicans mark already carries it.

issues.problem: Lent starts Feb 10, so fish fries and crawfish boil season begin just after Mardi Gras, not in "mid-March". Boil Season is also tied to a Play-In push that a 26-56 team may not have. And it overlaps with Super Sunday and St. Joseph's Night in the same weeks.
issues.fix: Start the Boil Season story in late February or early March, around the team's actual schedule. Keep the Play-In tee as a contingency only. Avoid Super Sunday weekend (Mar 14, 2027) and St. Joseph's Night (Mar 19) entirely.

issues.problem: The hoops and retail dossiers point to Xavier, Dillard, Southern and the HBCU fan base. They also point to LHSAA playoffs, when school pride peaks from February to March. Then there's the Sugar Bowl crowd, and Louisiana-wide Gulf South fans: Baton Rouge, Acadiana, the Gulf Coast. The brief uses none of these as a partner or window.
issues.fix: Add an HBCU capsule with Xavier and Dillard (and Southern and Grambling for Classic). Add a Friday-night school-rivalry home night timed to the LHSAA playoffs. Add a Gulf South regional product line sold outside the metro.

issues.problem: The underground dossier's St. Claude and Marigny layer (Zeitgeist, AllWays Lounge, Hi-Ho), drag and Southern Decadence are barely used. The actual courts (Joe W. Brown Park, Behrman) and the summer heat-led hooper's needs appear only as a heat note in the retail playbook.
issues.fix: Make one court-based event at Joe W. Brown or Behrman, with mesh and sleeveless product. Add a Southern Decadence or Halloween bounce night with the queer artists credited. Pitch both as paid collaborations, not drops.

issues.target: pulse and risks (Zion and Jordan Brand)
issues.problem: Zion is flagged as a Jordan Brand conflict, yet the brief still assigns him "kids swingman" and player tees in the holiday core. It lists the Murphy-first strategy without checking Nike's own relationships with Murphy, Queen and Fears. Player product depends on which of them Nike actually signs.
issues.fix: Confirm each player's apparel arrangement before assigning product. Run Zion pieces through Jordan Brand, and make the Nike-signed names the lead in the holiday plan. If that can't be confirmed, lead with city and ward product in the holiday window.

issues.problem: The brief says "sell the city, not the team" for a team whose product it also needs to move. The 56 opportunity score looks high given retail 34 and fandom 38. The plan also sets a 70% sell-through KPI by Feb 1 for a regional market with a small team-gear base.
issues.fix: Lower the sell-through target and set an expectation per tier (entry tees versus premium). Say how much of the plan is team-branded. Consider an opportunity score nearer the mid-40s.

strengths: The strategy puts the city mark first and the team mark second. It grounds that in real local behavior: phrase tees over team gear, ward and school identity, and the Saints and LSU competing for the same closet.

The Corner Tile concept (tile street names, iron-lace, sign-painter lettering, brass) passes the swap test. It avoids the Carnival palette the fan-favorite City Edition already owns, and keeps Black Masking Indian beadwork and ceremonial imagery out.

The calendar follows the city's own clock: king cake, Mardi Gras Day on Feb 9, 2027, second-line season, Essence, Jazz Fest. It sensibly keeps hero launches out of the two weeks before Carnival and away from Super Sunday and Aug 29.
The pay-and-credit stance is specific: parade fees, instruments through named programs, proceeds to community groups the artists choose, and credit on the product.
Weighting the plan toward city-first product that sells whatever the standings is the right call for a 26-56 team with a new coach and a thin retail base.
critique.summary: The brief is strong on culture and specificity, with a design language no other city could wear and a careful line on sacred material. Delivery is weaker. Corner Tile can't be the 2026-27 uniform, Ward Call is overloaded for an October launch, and NBA and NBPA licensing blocks the rapid-response tee. Fix the sequencing, let the communities set the terms, and cut the novelty items.
